families.Session: Checking the DOSBox-X build, starting a session, asking what state it is in, finding its window and ending it.
families.Machine: What the DOS machine holds at a stop (memory blocks, drivers, interrupt vectors) and what the program and the emulator write to the log.
families.Read: Reading what the stopped program holds: memory, registers, code, and which of its screens is showing.
families.Screen: Reading what the screen shows at a stop: its text or its picture, its colours, and a short hash of it.
families.Scan: Finding the address of a value nobody has named yet.
families.Write: Changing the machine: memory, a register, and any command the debugger takes.
families.Hardware: The hardware behind the cpu: I/O ports, the interrupt controllers and the A20 line.
families.Run: The tools that let the program run and stop it again.
families.Breakpoints: Breakpoints and watches the server saves by name and sets again in later sessions.
families.States: Saved states: the whole emulated machine written to a file, listed, and loaded back.
families.Names: Load your program's symbol table, look up a name or an address, and ask the knowledge base what a number is called.
families.Comments: Notes on addresses of the program, saved with the breakpoints and shown in the disassembly.
families.Input: Sending keys, mouse buttons and pointer moves to the DOS program, and checking that it reacted.
families.Captures: Saving the screen and the sound to files: a still, a series of frames, a video, a recording, and the list of them.
families.Files: Comparing pictures and recordings on disk, in numbers, and checking a file the DOS program wrote.
families.Sequences: Running several calls as one: a list of steps, an input with its check, and a session written as a replay script.
families.Project: Saving what a session learned into the repository's `.scry/` folder, after a review.

build_check.what: Check which DOSBox-X would run and whether it has the debugger a session needs, before starting one.
build_check.ask: Which DOSBox-X would you run, and does it have the debugger?
build_check.on: On any host where DOSBox-X is installed, before a session is open. It needs no program.
build_check.reads: The build has the debugger, and it has heavy debugging, the option `trace` needs.

arguments.binary: The DOSBox-X to check, as an absolute path. Left empty, `DOSBOX_X_BINARY`, else the `dosbox-x` on the PATH.

returns.binary_origin: Where its path came from: `argument`, `DOSBOX_X_BINARY` or `PATH`.
returns.version: The build's own version line, or `available: false` with a `why`: a version that cannot be read never fails the call.
returns.heavy_debug: Whether the build has heavy debugging, which `trace` and a `freeze` watch, one that holds bytes at their value, need. `false` is an answer, not a failure.
returns.debugger_commands: The optional debugger commands the build has; several tools need one. Left out when it has none.
returns.debugger_commands_missing: Each command the build lacks (`command`) with the tools that stop working without it (`disables`). Left out when none is missing.

refuses: A session is open: answering would start a second emulator (`session_live`).
A `binary` that is not an absolute path or names no executable (`bad_argument`).
`DOSBOX_X_BINARY` or the PATH naming no executable, or a build without the debugger (`host_failed`).
why: A DOSBox-X built without the debugger starts fine and then leaves `start` waiting until it gives up, so this check comes first. It reads the binary's own bytes and never asks it: `-helpdebug` lists `-break-start` on a build without the debugger too, and on Windows it prints nowhere and never exits.

It is refused while a session is open: reading the version starts a second emulator, which a build that does not know the option runs until the check gives up. The answer is about the build, never about a reading, and `debugger` is always `true`: a build without one is refused.
why_more:
`tools` lists this server's tools by name.

`presence_layers` lists the layers of `start`'s `overlay` the build draws: all six, five before the record mark, or the border and the pointer from an older build. It is left out without the `PRESENCE` command.

start.what: Start DOSBox-X from your conf file and leave the machine stopped at the debugger, at its first instruction.
start.ask: Start Bricks in a window I can watch without losing my keyboard, for at most fifteen minutes, and keep its log.
start.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds. The example session starts it for a person to watch, with a log file for what the game writes.
start.reads: The session may live 900 seconds (`bound_s`), and `watched` says it has a window. `kept` says the arguments were saved as a start profile, for `promote` to write into a repository.

arguments.conf: The DOSBox-X conf file to run, as it is. Required unless a start profile gives it.
arguments.cwd: The folder the conf's relative paths resolve in. Required unless a start profile gives it.
arguments.session_seconds: The session's lifetime in seconds, after which the emulator is ended. Required unless a start profile gives it.
arguments.shared: `true` when a person watches: the session opens a window. Left out, it has none.
arguments.display: Which display the window opens on, by the operating system's index. Needs `shared=true`; left out, 0, the main display.
arguments.fullscreen: `true` makes the window fill the display; DOSBox-X then captures the mouse, so its pointer no longer follows yours. Needs `shared=true`.
arguments.size: The window's size as `WIDTHxHEIGHT`, in the host's unit. Needs `shared=true`; left out, the conf's own size, else the largest 4:3 window the display holds.
arguments.flags: More command-line tokens for DOSBox-X, one list item each: `["-set", "cpu core=normal"]`. They come after the server's own, so a `-set` of the same key wins.
arguments.break_on_int3: `true` also stops at the program's own `int 3`, where a program marks a break. The stop at the debugger's first prompt still comes first.
arguments.program: A program to run inside DOS once the conf's `[autoexec]` has finished. Left empty, none.
arguments.logfile: A file that receives what the program writes to port `0xE9`, its own debug log, which `log` and `log_wait` read. A file already there is overwritten.
arguments.capture_video: `true` records the run of `program` as video, and the window shows the record mark until the program ends. It needs `program`.
arguments.captures_dir: Where the emulator writes a capture it takes itself. Left empty, `capture` under the working directory.
arguments.plan: A list of calls to run right after the start, each `{"op": <tool>, ...arguments}`, run as `perform` runs a list.
arguments.settle_seconds: How long each wait of the `plan` may take, in seconds. Left out, 30.
arguments.input_port: The TCP port the emulated COM1 dials, through which keys and mouse reach the program. Left at 0, a free one; any other is 1024 or above.
arguments.state_dir: The folder `state_write` saves into, which stays after `close`. Left empty, the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.
arguments.binary: The DOSBox-X to run: an executable, or on macOS a `.app` bundle holding one. Left empty, `DOSBOX_X_BINARY`, else the `dosbox-x` on the PATH.
arguments.background: `true` opens the window behind your other windows and leaves the keyboard focus where it is; `false` opens it in front. Left out, behind unless `shared`.
arguments.presence: Draws a border around the emulator's window while the session is open, brighter while a call runs the machine. `false` leaves it off.
arguments.overlay: Layers over the border, each on unless `false`: `calls` names each call, `keys` keys held, `pointer` the pointer, `pause` a stopped machine, `record` a recording. `place`: `top`, `bottom`, `auto`.
arguments.dos_calls: `true` records every DOS call (INT 21h) the program makes, for `log(channel="dos")`. It needs a build whose debugger has `DOSTRACE`.
arguments.log_categories: DOSBox-X's own `[log]` categories, each with its level, written into `logfile`. It needs `logfile`.
arguments.guest_files: Up to 16 files on the host that the program is expected to leave. `guest_file` and `close` say what became of each.
arguments.symbols: A symbol table, checked now and loaded at the first stop where DOS holds the program it is named after. `symbols_load` loads one later.
arguments.base_from: Where the table's addresses start: `program`, the program's own load address, or a segment register read at a protected-mode stop. Left out, `program`.
arguments.profile: A start profile: a saved set of `start` arguments, by its name under `.scry/start/` or by a path. It fills only the arguments the call leaves out.
arguments.names: `false` leaves a reply's numbers bare, with no `names` field, no name in its summary and no note on a disassembled line; the window's captions still name them.

returns.window: With `shared`, where the window is. Its `front` is `true` when no other application's window covers its centre; it does not mean the window has the keyboard focus.
returns.input_port: The TCP port the emulated COM1 dialled, or why no input connection was opened.
returns.symbols: With `symbols`: `held`, the table's path; `base_from`; and `checked`, what comparing it with the executable beside it found.
returns.profile: With a start profile: its `name`, its `file`, and `supplied`, the arguments it filled.
returns.kept: Says that this start's arguments were saved as a start profile for `promote`, the tool that writes one into your repository's `.scry/` folder.
returns.start: With `plan`: the start's own fields sit here, beside the plan's account of its steps.

refuses: A session is already open (`session_live`).
`conf`, `cwd` or `session_seconds` given neither by the call nor by a start profile, or a path that is not absolute (`bad_argument`).
A conf, a `cwd` or a `logfile` folder that does not exist, or a `symbols` table the executable beside it contradicts (`bad_argument`).
`display`, `fullscreen` or `size` without `shared=true`, or a `display` the host does not have (`bad_argument`).
A `size` that does not fit the display, comes with `fullscreen`, or is ignored by the conf's `sdl output` (`bad_argument`).
`fullscreen` under `sdl output=surface`, or on macOS on a display other than 0 (`bad_argument`).
`flags` that set what a named argument owns, or a `-set` glued to its value or without `=` (`bad_argument`).
`capture_video` without `program`, `log_categories` without `logfile`, an `input_port` from 1 to 1023, or `guest_files` naming a folder, a file twice or more than 16 (`bad_argument`).
A `profile` that no `.scry/` folder searched holds; `searched` lists them (`bad_argument`).
`dos_calls` on a build whose debugger has no `DOSTRACE` command (`no_channel`).
A window that never appears on the display asked for. The session stays open for `window` or `close` (`window_not_visible`).
A DOSBox-X that exits or never reaches its debugger (`session_broken`).
why: `shared` says whether a person watches. Without it the session has no window at all, and `window` cannot report one. With it the window opens on `display`, in front; add `background=true` to watch without losing the keyboard focus.

A start profile is a file of `start` arguments, `.scry/start/<name>.json` in a repository, so a session starts with `start(profile="<name>")`. The call's own arguments win and the profile fills the rest. The `.scry/` folder is looked for upwards from the server's working directory, then from `cwd`.

The server runs the conf you name as it is and writes none of its own. It mounts its own folder on a drive letter the conf's `[autoexec]` leaves free and runs `SCRY.COM` from it, the helper that delivers keys and mouse inside DOS. So the conf must not `exit` before `program` runs.
why_more:
| you want | arguments | the window |
|---|---|---|
| Nobody watching | `shared=false`, the default | None. `window` refuses it as `no_channel`. |
| Somebody watching | `shared=true`, with `display` and `size` or `fullscreen` if wanted | On the display, in front, confirmed in the host's window list. |
| Watching and keeping the keyboard focus | `shared=true`, `background=true` | The same, opened behind your other windows. |
**The window's size.**

A windowed session opens 40 px inside the display's corner. Its size is `size` when given, else the conf's `windowresolution`, else the largest 4:3 window the display's usable area holds. The menu bar, Dock and taskbar do not count as usable.

`size` is in the host's unit: points on macOS, real pixels on Windows. Every OpenGL output and Direct3D take a size, and so does an unset `output` on macOS and Windows; `surface` does not. Under an output that ignores it, `size` is refused, and without `size` the conf's size stays.

`fullscreen` under `sdl output=surface` is refused because that output fills the display by switching its video mode, and the window ends off screen. On macOS it is accepted on display 0 only: a start stopped at its first instruction reaches full screen on another display only once the program runs.
`start` waits until the host lists the window on that display. It does not check the size, since a stopped window keeps the conf's size until the program runs; `window` does.

`background` only chooses where the window opens. How the focus stays with you is the host's: on macOS the emulator starts as a background application, and on Windows no program may take the foreground while `start` launches. A click or ALT moves the focus as always.
On Windows a start in front brings its window forward once it is up, and `window.front` says whether Windows allowed it.
**The lifetime.**

`session_seconds` is a hard limit because DOSBox-X's own time limit counts emulated time, which a machine stopped at the debugger never spends. A watchdog process, `scry-dosbox-x-guardian` in the process list, keeps the host's clock instead. It ends the emulator a few seconds past the limit, or soon after this server dies.
**Flags.**

- A flag that sets what a named argument sets (`-time-limit`, `sdl videodriver`, `log logfile`, the conf, the program) is refused, naming the argument: coming after the server's, it would undo it.
- So is a `-set` of `sdl display`, `sdl fullscreen`, `sdl windowposition` or `sdl windowresolution`, and `-fullscreen`.
- A `-set` value with spaces is one token. A `-set` glued to its value is refused because DOSBox-X hangs on it.
- A `-set` without `=` is refused because DOSBox-X ignores it with no error, and the setting would not apply.
- `key=value` with no section is accepted, and a key the server owns is refused in that spelling too.
- Without a window the server passes `videodriver=dummy`. It never passes `-silent`, which exits after `AUTOEXEC.BAT` and cannot keep a session open.
**The program and its symbols.**

- `program` loads the input helper itself when the conf's autoexec does not run it. A copy of `SCRY.COM` in the conf that speaks another protocol is reported in the `note`.
- A `symbols` table is compared with the executable beside it before anything starts. `symbols.checked` says how many global code symbols agreed, or why nothing could be compared.
- It is compared again at the first stop that holds the program, since the executable can be rebuilt meanwhile. That stop's reply carries `symbols_placed`, once.
- `symbols_placed` holds `placed`, `path`, `load_segment` in real mode, `base` and `loaded`; a refusal is `placed: false` with `code` and `why`.
- `base_from=program` is the DOS load segment of a real-mode program. For a DJGPP COFF executable it is the selector `CS` holds at a protected-mode stop, where the code runs.
- `break_on_int3` has two limits that are the debugger's: an `int 3` at the reset vector faults, and one at the address of a stop is stepped over by `resume`.
- `guest_files` answers each file as `path` and `before`, what it was before the boot.
**Speed.**

`[cpu] use dynamic core with fpu` decides whether FPU code runs recompiled. Its `auto` takes FPU and MMX instructions off the dynamic core. A single-tasking DOS program that leans on the FPU then runs below real time with nothing in the session saying so, and a conf for it states `true`.
**What else the reply says.**

- `captures_dir` and `state_dir` are created with their parents. `state_dir` in the reply is the folder in use.
- `shared`, `ready_after_s`, `argv`, `binary`, `binary_origin`, `version`, `background` and `presence` say what the launch used.
- A `version` the build would not give is `available: false` with a `why`, and never fails the start.
- `rearm_refused` says why saved raw breakpoints could not be set again.
- No free drive letter for the input helper is refused before anything starts.
**Files, the emulator's log and the border.**

- A file a tool reads must be a regular file, never a folder. A tool never writes over a file unless its entry says it replaces one, as `logfile` does.
- `logfile` is written under a name of lowercase words joined by hyphens, as every file the server writes, so a capital or a `%` in it is replaced.
- At `debug` a `log_categories` category can write a line per event: `files` writes one per read once the `[log]` setting `fileio` is on. Turn on only what the question needs.
- The border never changes another reply: a failure to draw it shows only in `presence`, in `start` and `status`; `overlay` says which of its layers are drawn.
- While the debugger does not answer, the border is not redrawn. It catches up once a call is answered.

status.what: Ask whether a session is open and what the machine is doing, without moving it.
status.ask: Is the emulator still up, and where is it stopped?
status.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), right after that start: the machine is stopped at its first instruction.
status.reads: The machine is stopped in real mode at `F000:0000FFF0`, the reset vector. `pending` is empty, so nothing waits for the next stop, and `declarations` counts no saved breakpoint or watch.

returns.last_stop: Where the machine last stopped: its `pc` and `cause`, and `since_s`, how long ago. Unavailable, with why, when there is no stop to report.
returns.pc: Where the machine stands now (`SSSS:OOOOOOOO`), read from the registers, so a `set_register` on `CS:IP` shows here; `cpu_mode` is beside it. Unavailable while running.
returns.stopped_on_its_own: Present when the machine had stopped and no call had reported it yet. `status` records that stop as the last one.
returns.pending: What waits for the next stop: `arm`, the breakpoints declared while the program ran; a `disarm` count; and whether a `symbols_load` or a `base_remeasure` is queued.
returns.symbols_held: Present while a `start` symbol table waits for its program: its `path`, its `base_from` and `waiting_for`, the program's file name.
returns.knowledge: How many entries `knowledge_find` answers (`served`), and how many it holds and does not answer yet (`held_back`).

why: `status` answers in every state: with no session, while the machine runs and once the session is broken. It is where you learn why another tool does not answer.
At a stop it also sets the breakpoints that were declared while the program ran, and says so in `applied_on_stop`.
`session` carries five warnings, each only while it is true: `program`, `range_widened`, `conf_changed_on_disk`, `image_changed_on_disk` and `output_bytes_dropped`.
why_more:
- `conf_changed_on_disk`: the conf file changed since `start`. It is `false` too when the file is gone.
- `image_changed_on_disk`: the executable the loaded symbol table was checked against was written since, as a rebuild under an open session does.
- `output_bytes_dropped`: the emulator printed more than the server keeps.
- `program`: the program that ran inside DOS is gone. It is `state: exited` with `name` and `seen_by`, or `state: fault` with `fault`, the message DJGPP writes as a program dies.
- `program` is read at the stops that answer a call, never while the program runs, so a session that never stops never learns it.

- `presence` is `true` when the border is drawn, `false` when it was asked off, or the reason it is not drawn.
- `overlay` comes with a drawn border: the `layers` drawn, the `place` of the captions and, per layer the build cannot draw, `lacking` with the reason.
- `declarations` counts the server's own saved `breakpoints`, `watches` and `regpoints` (stops on a register condition).
- `last_stop` also carries `stop_seq` and `wall_at`.
- `pid`, `conf`, `conf_digest`, `watched`, `bound_s`, `elapsed_s`, `captures`, `state_dir` and `bundle` describe the process, as `start` set it up.

window.what: Find where the session's window is on your displays and whether another window covers it, or bring it in front.
window.ask: Where is the emulator's window, and can I see it?
window.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), started with `shared=true` so that it has a window to report.
window.reads: The run hides the `window` block and the summary here, because where the window is differs on every host. `status` is `ok`: the host listed the window.

arguments.front: `true` brings the window in front of whatever covers it and reads the result back. Left out, the window is reported where it is and nothing moves.

returns.window: Where it is: `display`, `bounds`, `onscreen`, `fullscreen` and `front`. `front` is `true` when no other application's window covers its centre; it does not mean the window has the keyboard focus.
returns.size: Only when `start` named a `size`: what was `asked`, what is `seen`, and whether it `matches` within `tolerance_px`.

refuses: No session is open (`no_session`).
The session's emulator died (`session_broken`).
The session was started without `shared`, so there is no watched window to report (`no_channel`).
The window never appears, or with `front` is still covered after it was activated. `seen` says what the host listed (`window_not_visible`).
why: `front` answers one question: can a person see the picture? It is `true` when the window is on screen and no other application's window covers its centre. It is not the keyboard focus, which a window nothing covers can be without.

`window` answers at any time, a running program included. Without `front` it moves nothing and reports the window wherever you put it. With `front`, a session started with `background=true` may stay behind, and the refusal names that as the likely cause.

A `size` given to `start` is checked here and not there, because the window takes that size at the program's first video mode. Until the program has run it reads the emulator's own size, and the `note` says to `resume` and ask again. The size the server chose by itself is never checked.
why_more:
- `compared` says which rectangle was measured: `client`, the area inside the frame, on Windows; `outer` on macOS, which has no client area, so a title bar's height is allowed.
- `height_free` is `true` when the emulator fits the height to the picture's aspect by itself, so only the width is checked.
- `display` is the operating system's index, and `fullscreen` is `true` when the window's bounds are the display's.
- On a `window_not_visible` refusal, `asked_display` is the display `start` asked for and `activation` what bringing it forward answered.

close.what: End the session and the emulator with it, and learn how it ended.
close.ask: We are done: close the emulator and tell me how it ended.
close.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), at the end of the example session's session.
close.reads: DOSBox-X quit when asked, with exit code 0. `omitted` names the last lines it printed, which a clean quit leaves out.

arguments.detail: `true` returns the last lines the emulator printed (`stdout_tail`, `errorlog_tail`) after a clean quit too. Left out, they come only when the end was not clean.

returns.closed: `true` when a session was ended; `false` when there was none to close.
returns.exit_code: The emulator's exit code. It is `available: false` with a `why` when no session was running or the killed process could not be collected.
returns.pid: The process this call ended, or `available: false` with a `why` when no session was running.
returns.guest_files: Each file `start` named in `guest_files`, with the `state` that `guest_file` reports for it.
returns.draft: The names of what the session saved and `promote` has not yet written into your repository's `.scry/` folder.

why: `close` ends the session now instead of leaving it to `session_seconds`. It asks DOSBox-X to quit and kills it only when the request is ignored; `ended_by` says which happened.
`session` describes the state after the close: `alive`, `running` and `altered` are `false`, as with no session.
The reply also says what the process was, in `status`'s fields, read before the end. So `pid` is the process this call ended.
why_more:
- `quit`: DOSBox-X left when asked. A session started here does, with or without a program loaded, because `start` turns its quit warning off.
- `killed`: a conf that turns the warning back on, or a program that ignored the request. `exit_code` is unavailable if the process is still not collected.
- `died`: it had already exited.
- `none`: there was no session.

- The request is SIGTERM on macOS and the debugger's `QUIT` on Windows, which has no signal to ask with; the kill is SIGKILL, or a terminate on Windows.
- A `note` says the emulator's output was not read to its end, so the last lines may be short.

machine_map.what: Get the layout of the DOS machine at this stop: its memory blocks, device drivers, extended memory handles and the cpu's control registers.
machine_map.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, stopped at its play screen.
machine_map.ask: List the blocks of memory DOS holds right now.
machine_map.reads: In real mode the debugger's `DOS MCBS` listing gave 9 memory blocks, and none was cut from the reply. Their rows are too long to show here: the whole reply, below, has them.

arguments.sections: Which sections to read. Left out, all of them but `bios_mem`, `callbacks`, `paging` and `vga`.
arguments.dest: A file to write every row of the sections read, as JSON: an absolute or `~` path that does not exist yet. Left empty, no file is written.

returns.cpu_mode: `real`, `protected` or `paged`, read from the control register `cr0`. It decides which sections exist.
returns.mcbs: DOS's chain of memory blocks, one row each: `memory`, `mcb_seg`, `size_bytes`, `psp_seg`, `notes`, `filename`.
returns.coverage_note: Why each absent section is absent: the mode has none, or the debugger's listing could not be read.
returns.sources: For each section, the debugger command its rows came from.
returns.counts: How many rows each section has in full, so a list cut short shows.
returns.truncated: `true` when a section had more than 400 rows and its list was cut; `dest` gets them all.

refuses: An empty `sections`, a name that is no section, or a `dest` that already exists (`bad_argument`).
A program that is running: the listings are read at a stop (`not_stopped`).
A listing longer than the debugger hands back in one reply: it would come back cut (`unexpected_answer`).
why: Each section is one listing of the debugger, read whole. A section the debugger refused, or printed in a form the server does not know, is absent, never partial. A chain of memory blocks with one block skipped would read as the whole chain.
Which sections exist depends on the cpu mode. In real mode `gdt` and `ldt` are absent, because there the debugger reads the interrupt vector table as descriptors; `paging` exists only with paging on.
`cpu_mode` comes from `cr0`, which cannot tell virtual 8086 mode from protected mode. At such a stop it says `protected` where the stop's own reply and `status` say `VM86`.
why_more:
- `mcbs`: a free block has a `psp_seg` of `0000` and keeps in `filename` the old name DOS left there.
- The chain in `mcbs` is checked by its sizes, each block right after the one before; a chain that fails is absent.
- `devs`: `header`, `attr`, `strat`, `intr`, `name`.
- `kern`: `seg`, `size_bytes`, `what`.
- `xms`: `handle`, `status`, `location`, `size_bytes`.
- `ems`: `handle`, `addr`, `size_bytes`, `name`. `ems_pages`: `handle`, `page`, `start`, `end`.
- `bios_mem`: `start`, `end`, `status`, `what`. `callbacks`: `number`, `desc`.
- `control`: `cr0`, `cr2`, `cr3`, `cpl`, `eflags`, `vm`, `iopl`, `nt`, `gdtr`, `idt`, `tr`, `ldtr`.
- `gdt` and `ldt`: `selector`, `base`, `limit`, `type`, `dpl`, `p`, `a`, `r`, `b`, `g`.
- `paging`: runs of pages next to each other in linear and physical memory with the same flags: `start`, `end`, `phy`, `flags`, `d`, `a`.
- `vga`: `mode`, `crtc`, `seq`, `gc`, `ac`, `dac`, `draw`.
- `emu_mem` holds the emulator's memory listing, a key per line; `machine` is the emulated machine's name.
- Each listing is one exchange with the debugger. `omitted` and `how` name the sections of this mode that were not read.
- When the listing behind `control` cannot be read, `cpu_mode` is unavailable and `gdt`, `ldt` and `paging` are absent.

interrupt_vectors.what: See which handler each interrupt vector points at, and which program, DOS block or BIOS block holds that handler.
interrupt_vectors.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, stopped at its play screen.
interrupt_vectors.ask: Who handles the mouse interrupt, INT 33h?
interrupt_vectors.reads: INT 33h points at `C402:0010`, inside the memory block at segment 9FFF, which is marked as DOS's. Of the 256 vectors, 112 sit in a known block (`held`) and none has a symbol (`named`).

arguments.number: One vector to return, `0x00` to `0xFF`, as an integer or `0x` text. Left out, all 256 come back.

returns.vectors: One row per vector: `number`, the handler's `seg_off` and linear `addr`, the block that holds it under `mcbs`, `kern` or `bios_mem`, and the nearest `symbol`.
returns.counts: `vectors`, how many the table has; `held`, how many sit in a known block; `named`, how many have a symbol.
returns.cpu_mode: The mode at this stop: `real`, `VM86`, `protected` or `paged`. In protected mode the table read is the IDT.
returns.coverage_note: What could not be worked out, and why: a vector with no `addr`, a handler no block holds, a table still empty.
returns.sources: The debugger command behind the vectors and behind each listing the blocks came from.

refuses: A `number` outside `0x00` to `0xFF` (`bad_argument`).
A file named `MCPIVT.TXT` already in the emulator's working directory: move it aside, it is never deleted (`bad_argument`).
A program that is running (`not_stopped`).
A table the debugger did not write whole, or a listing too long for one reply (`unexpected_answer`).
why: Each handler is matched to the block of memory that holds it, so the reply says which program hooked a vector with no earlier table to compare. The first block holding the address wins: `mcbs`, then `kern`, then `bios_mem`.
Right after `start` every vector reads `0000:0000`: DOS has not filled the table yet.
`symbol` is what `symbols_find(linear=...)` answers for the handler, given only between the table's lowest and highest symbol.
why_more: The debugger writes the table to a file, `MCPIVT.TXT`, which the server reads and removes. The whole table is read even for one `number`, with the listings `machine_map` reads, one exchange with the debugger each.

log.what: Read the newest log lines that match a pattern: the program's, the emulator's, both, or the DOS calls the program made.
log.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, started with `logfile`, after a ball was served and lost.
log.ask: What did the game log about serves, hits and lost balls?
log.reads: Six lines of the game's own log match, oldest first. Each opens with `Bochs port E9h:`, the emulator's mark on a line the program wrote to port 0xE9.

arguments.pattern: A regular expression each line is searched for. It is never empty: `.` matches every line.
arguments.channel: Which log to read. `guest` is the program's port 0xE9 lines, `emulator` DOSBox-X's own, `all` both with each line tagged, `dos` the program's INT 21h calls.
arguments.limit: How many of the newest matching lines to return: 1 to 400. Left out, 40.
arguments.labels: `true` adds `labels`: the lines returned, counted by their first word. Left out, no count.
arguments.since_mark: A byte position in the log: only lines written after it are read. Left out or 0, the whole log is read.

returns.lines: The newest `limit` matching lines, oldest first. Not on `dos`.
returns.lines_total: How many lines matched in all, not how many came back.
returns.truncated: `true` when more matched than came back.
returns.labels: With `labels=true`, the returned lines counted by their first word: a quick view of who is writing.
returns.calls: On `dos`, the matching calls in place of `lines`, each with the registers DOS took, the ones it handed back and its result.
returns.calls_dropped: On `dos`, how many of the oldest calls the server no longer holds.

refuses: An empty pattern, or one that is not a regular expression (`bad_argument`).
A `limit` outside 1 to 400 (`bad_argument`).
A session started without `logfile`, a log not written yet, or `guest` on a log with no line from the program (`no_channel`).
`dos` on a session not started with `dos_calls` (`no_channel`).
`dos` with `labels` or `since_mark`: the calls are not lines of the log file (`bad_argument`).
`channel` `process`: the emulator's own output is not a log; `close(detail=true)` returns its last lines (`bad_argument`).
A `since_mark` past the end of the log (`bad_argument`).
why: `guest`, `emulator` and `all` are three views of one file, so one `since_mark` position serves all three. `all` is the file in order, each line tagged `[guest] ` or `[emulator] `.

`dos` is another record: every INT 21h call the program made, with its result, on a session started with `dos_calls`. There `pattern` is matched against each call's `line` and `lines_total` counts calls.

An empty `lines` is an answer: nothing matched. A log with no line from the program at all is refused, so that silence is never read as no match. While the program runs a line it has only now written may not be in the file yet, and `note` says so.
why_more:
- On `dos`, each call is two rows of the debugger's `DOSTRACE`, one as DOS takes it and one as DOS hands it back, paired by number.
- On `dos`, each call of `calls` holds `in` and `out`, the registers DOS took and handed back; `out.cf` is the carry flag.
- `error` is the code and its name, for the calls that report failure by the carry: AH 38h and up. An older call answers in AL and gets none.
- `returned` is `false` for a call DOS has not handed back yet, as at a stop inside it.
- `switched: true` marks a call that never returned to its caller, as an EXEC or an exit: the registers are then another program's, so no result is claimed.
- The emulator's own `int21` and `fileio` lines, switched on in the conf's `[log]` section, are written before DOS runs the call, so they never carry its result.
- `time_s` and `returned_s` are seconds of emulated time since power-on, the clock `run_for` reports.

log_wait.what: Wait until a log line matches a pattern, or get the line at once when the log already has it.
log_wait.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, started with `logfile` and running, a ball served and nobody at the paddle.
log_wait.ask: Wait up to a minute for the game to log that the ball was lost.
log_wait.reads: `TARGET` means a line matched within the minute: the game logged `LOST`, a line of its own, written to port 0xE9.

arguments.pattern: A regular expression each line is searched for. It is never empty: `.` matches every line.
arguments.channel: Which log to wait on: `guest`, `emulator`, `all` or `dos`, as in [`log`](#log).
arguments.seconds: How long to wait at most, in seconds, up to 600. Left out, 30.
arguments.since_mark: A byte position in the log: only lines written after it count, the ones already there included. Left out or 0, the whole log counts.

returns.verdict: `TARGET` when a line matched, `TIMEOUT` when the time ran out with none; `note` then says what was read.
returns.line: The first line that matched; for the newest one, use `log`. On `dos`, `call` holds the matching call in its place.
returns.already: `true` when the log held the line before the call, so nothing was waited for.
returns.waited_s: Seconds spent waiting; 0 when the line was already there.
returns.arrived_during: How many lines were written during the wait, whether or not they matched.
returns.lines_examined: How many lines were read in all: those the log held and those that came during the wait. On `dos`, the calls the server holds.

refuses: A machine stopped at the debugger, or one that stops during the wait, while the log lacks the line. It logs nothing, and `last_stop` says where it stopped (`wait_stopped`).
An emulator that exits during the wait (`session_broken`).
`seconds` out of range, an empty or malformed pattern, or a `since_mark` past the end of the log (`bad_argument`).
A session started without `logfile` (`no_channel`).
`dos` on a session not started with `dos_calls` (`no_channel`).
`dos` with a `since_mark` (`bad_argument`).
why: The log is read before any waiting, so a line written before the call is found at once, where a tool that only waited would report that it never came. `already` marks such a line.

A `TIMEOUT` says what it read. `arrived_during` counts the lines written during the wait and `lines_examined` every line read, so a program that wrote nothing is told apart from one whose lines did not match.

A log that does not exist yet is not refused: that is the state right after `resume`. When the wait returns the program is usually still running: use the line to choose an address for `run_to` or `watch_add` on the next run.
why_more:
- `lines_before` counts the lines read before the match and `lines_total` the matches in that read. On `dos` both count calls, and `calls_dropped` the oldest ones the server let go.
- A debugger that does not answer, inside a long host call, is asked once, and then only the file is read. A `TIMEOUT` says the run state is unknown.
- No breakpoint can be set on a log line; the nearest is a watch for changes on the variable whose change produces it.
- `expect` on `send_keys` and `drive` is this wait on `guest`, from a position taken before the keys are sent.

registers.what: Read the cpu's registers, now or as they were at the last stop.
registers.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped at `brick_hit` as the ball knocks out its first brick.
registers.ask: Show me the cpu's registers at this stop.
registers.reads: Fifteen registers came back. The whole reply, folded below, lists each under `regs` as a hex string.

arguments.from_last_stop: `true` returns the registers the last stop recorded, and answers while the program runs. Left out, the registers are read now.

returns.regs: Each register by name, as a hex string of its own width.
returns.superseded: `true` with `from_last_stop`: the values are the last stop's, which `last_stop` identifies, not the current ones.

refuses: `from_last_stop` before the session's first stop (`no_stop`).
why: `CR0`, `CR3` and the descriptor tables are not here: `machine_map(sections=["control"])` reads them.

read_memory.what: Read a few bytes of memory at an address, as hex text.
read_memory.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen before any brick falls, with its symbols loaded.
read_memory.ask: Read the two bytes of the score.
read_memory.reads: `score` is at `08DF:00000615` (`seg_off`) and holds `0000`: no point scored yet.

arguments.ref: The address to read: a symbol or a `SEG:OFF` address.
arguments.length: How many bytes: 1 to 128. Left out, 16.

returns.hex: The bytes, two hex characters each, lowest address first.
returns.seg_off: The address `ref` resolved to, as segment and offset.

refuses: A symbol the loaded table lacks (`unknown_ref`), or one it holds twice (`ambiguous_ref`).
An offset the cpu's mode cannot address: past `0xFFFF` in real mode (`bad_argument`).
A dump that is not the size asked for (`readback_refused`).
why: The bytes come from the debugger's `MEMDUMPBIN` of exactly that range, and a dump of any other size is refused, never handed back shifted. For more than 128 bytes, `memdump` writes a file.

disassemble.what: Disassemble the code at an address, one instruction a line, each marked as a call, a branch, a return or none of those.
disassemble.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen with its symbols loaded and a comment written on `brick_hit`.
disassemble.ask: Show me the first instructions of the routine that runs when a brick is hit.
disassemble.reads: Four 16-bit instructions from `brick_hit`; the first ends with the comment written on it. `flow` marks the third as a `call` and the others as `sequential`, plain instructions.

arguments.ref: Where to start: a symbol or a `SEG:OFF` address.
arguments.length: How many bytes to decode, 1 to 1024; left out, 16. The last instruction is completed even when it runs past them.

returns.lines: One x86 instruction a line: `SSSS:OOOOOOOO`, its bytes, its text. A line with a comment ends ` // <text>`.
returns.flow: One word per line: `call`, `branch`, `return`, `sequential` or `unknown`, as the decoder (`flow_source`, `capstone`) classified it.
returns.code_bits: 16 or 32, the width the code was decoded in. `code_bits_from` says where that width was read.
returns.resolved: Only with symbols loaded: each direct call or branch target and memory operand, with its address and nearest symbol. Rows carry `line`, `operand`, `kind`, `register`, `seg_off`, `addr`, `symbol` and `delta`.
returns.seg_off: The address `ref` resolved to, as segment and offset.
returns.line_notes: Where the base names an operand: `line`, `note`, and `live` when a register named it. A person's comment stays on its line.

refuses: A `length` that runs past the end of a 16-bit segment, where the cpu wraps; the refusal names the most bytes that fit (`bad_argument`).
The null selector, or one with no descriptor, in protected mode (`bad_argument`).
A symbol the loaded table lacks (`unknown_ref`), or one it holds twice (`ambiguous_ref`).
Whatever `memdump` refuses: the bytes are read the same way.
why: The debugger has no disassembly command, so capstone decodes the bytes read from memory. A byte no instruction starts with is listed as `.byte 0x..` and marked `unknown`.

The width is the segment's own, never the cpu mode's alone. Real mode is 16-bit; protected mode takes it from the stop for `CS`, from `SELINFO` for a segment another register holds, and from the descriptor tables otherwise.
why_more: In `resolved`, `kind` is `target` or `memory`. A memory operand is read through the segment register named in `register`, as it stands at this stop. Outside the loaded table's range, `symbol` and `delta` are unavailable.
**Checked against the debugger's own disassembly**

Each listing is checked line by line against the debugger's own code pane, and its bytes against what `read_memory` reads. The two agree on address, length, bytes, mnemonic and operands, and may differ in spelling alone:

- One instruction under two names: `jc` and `jb`, `jnc` and `jae`, `popad` and `popal`, `call` and `lcall` for a far call.
- A string instruction's implicit operands, which the pane leaves out, and a size word it leaves out where a register fixes the size.
- A symbol the pane prints in place of an operand's number.
- `FE /7`, which is no x86 instruction: DOSBox-X enters its own code through `FE 38`, so the pane reads it as `callback`. Here it is a byte no instruction starts with.

call_stack.what: Guess the chain of calls that led to the stop, by following the frame pointers on the stack.
call_stack.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped at `brick_hit` as the ball knocks out its first brick.
call_stack.ask: Who called the routine the game is stopped in?
call_stack.reads: One call, the stop itself in `brick_hit`. Bricks keeps no frame pointer, so no caller is found, and `ended_why` says where the chain broke.

returns.calls: One row per call, innermost first; row 0 is the stop. Each has `seg_off`, `addr`, `symbol`, `delta`, `via`, `call` and `bp`.
returns.heuristic: Always `true`: the chain is a guess, never proof of who called whom.
returns.ended_why: Why the chain ends where it does.
returns.truncated: `true` when the chain was cut at the most rows a reply lists, with frames still to read.
returns.code_bits: 16 or 32, the width of the code at the stop.

refuses: A stop whose registers came back without `SS`, `ESP` or `EBP` (`unexpected_answer`).
why: A routine that keeps no frame pointer shows its caller's caller in its place, or nothing.

At a routine's `push bp` or `enter`, the `mov bp, sp` after it, or its `ret`, the stop is outside the frame. The caller is then read from the stack pointer, and its row says `via` `entry`. The other rows come from the frame chain (`bp_chain`), near or far as the call before each says.

The chain ends at a saved frame pointer that is zero or does not rise, or at a frame past the stack segment's end. A return address no call precedes ends it unlisted; one outside the loaded symbol table ends it listed.
why_more: `call` is unavailable on row 0, and `bp` on row 0 and on an `entry` row.

memdump.what: Write a range of memory to a file, for ranges too large to read into the conversation.
memdump.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen before any brick falls, with its symbols loaded.
memdump.ask: Save the 60 bytes of the wall of bricks to a file.
memdump.reads: The file holds 60 bytes, as asked: `bytes` equals `length`. `path` is where it was written.

arguments.ref: Where the range begins: a symbol or a `SEG:OFF` address.
arguments.length: How many bytes to write, 1 or more.
arguments.dest: The file to create: an absolute or `~`-led path, not there yet.

returns.path: The file as written; a `note` says so when its name is not the one `dest` gave.
returns.seg_off: The address `ref` resolved to, as segment and offset.

refuses: A dump file already in the emulator's working folder, or a file already at `dest` (`bad_argument`).
A `dest` directly in the emulator's working folder, or at or under one of the debugger's own file names (`bad_argument`).
In protected mode: a range past `0xFFFF` on a 16-bit segment, a range past the segment's limit, or a selector with no descriptor (`bad_argument`).
In real mode: a range that ends past `FFFF:FFFF` (`bad_argument`).
A symbol the loaded table lacks (`unknown_ref`), or one it holds twice (`ambiguous_ref`).
A dump that is not `length` bytes (`readback_refused`).
why: The debugger writes the dump in the emulator's working folder, as `MCPDUMP.BIN`, and the server moves it to `dest`. A dump file already there is somebody's, so the call refuses it and deletes nothing; a dangling link counts. A `dest` in that folder is refused too: once moved, the file could not be told from a leftover.

Past offset `0xFFFF` the debugger would reread the start of a 16-bit segment, or write zeros past a segment's limit, and still report success. So in real mode a long range is read in 64 KiB pieces, up to `FFFF:FFFF`. In protected mode it is checked against the segment's descriptor first.
Inside offsets 0 to `0xFFFF` the segment's limit is not checked, and the debugger writes zeros past it.
why_more: Some builds of DOSBox-X name the file `MEMDUMP.BIN` themselves, in the working folder or in the captures folder, so a leftover of that name is refused in both. A `dest` is compared with those names on the file system, not by spelling. `captures_dir` is not where a dump lands.
Deleting a leftover first would not be safer. A delete that failed quietly would leave the old file, the debugger would still report success, and a stale dump would come back as new.

find.what: Find every address in a range of memory that holds a given sequence of bytes.
find.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen with its symbols loaded.
find.ask: Find where the program holds the text SCORE.
find.reads: The five bytes of `SCORE` are at one address, `08DF:00000601`. `span` says which bytes were searched: 1384 from `08DF:00000100`, the symbol `start`.

arguments.data_hex: The bytes to look for, as hex: whole bytes, at least one.
arguments.ref: Where the range begins: a symbol or a `SEG:OFF` address.
arguments.length: How many bytes to search from `ref`.

returns.hits: The addresses where the bytes begin, as `SEG:OFF`, at most 400; past that, the highest are kept.
returns.hits_total: How many addresses hold the bytes, listed or not.
returns.truncated: `true` when there are more hits than `hits` lists.
returns.span: The bytes that were searched, as `from`, `length` and `source`, so zero hits says where there are none. `source` is always `ref+length`.

refuses: Hex that is not whole bytes, or a `length` shorter than the bytes to find (`bad_argument`).
A symbol the loaded table lacks (`unknown_ref`), or one it holds twice (`ambiguous_ref`).
Whatever `memdump` refuses: the range is read the same way.
why: The debugger has no search for bytes. So the range is read as `memdump` reads it, into a temporary file that is gone before the reply, and searched there.
In real mode a hit past offset `0xFFFF` is written with a segment of its own, since no offset reaches it from the segment you gave.

screen_map_find.what: Name the screen your program is showing, from its screen map: a file of the program's screens and the named areas of each.
screen_map_find.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen with the game's own map loaded, as in the example of `screen_map_write` below.
screen_map_find.ask: Which screen is the game showing?
screen_map_find.reads: The game shows `play`, a screen of the loaded file (`layer` `file`). Its area `court` is the rectangle at 200, 80, with its centre at 240, 100.

returns.matched: `true` when a screen of the map is the one showing.
returns.screen: The name of the screen that matched.
returns.controls: The matched screen's named areas, each with `name`, `rect` and `centre`, in the program's own units.
returns.layer: Where the screen was found: `session` for a screen added in this session, `file` for one of the loaded map.
returns.screens_mapped: When nothing matched: how many screens the map holds. `screens_tried` says how many had the right kind and size.
returns.view_fits: `false` when the picture's size cannot be the map's, seen through the `scale` and `margin` it was loaded with.

refuses: No screen mapped yet: load a map or add a screen with `screen_map_write` (`needs_call`).
A video mode `screen_view` cannot read (`no_channel`).
why: A screen matches when its kind and size are the ones showing and each of its regions has the fingerprint the map recorded. Screens added this session are tried first, then the loaded file's.

The areas of the matched screen are what `send_mouse(target=)` clicks by name. The click acts on the screen this tool last matched, and what is drawn is not compared again. After anything that may have changed the screen, call it again at a stop.
A screen added with `cells` `index` is compared by palette index, not by colour.

screen_map_write.what: Build the screen map, the file that names your program's screens and their areas: add the screen showing, load a file, or save one.
screen_map_write.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, at any moment: a `load` reads a file, whether or not the game runs.
screen_map_write.ask: Load the screen map of Bricks.
screen_map_write.reads: The map of `bricks` holds one screen and one named area. Its `mode` is `verified`: a screen is checked each time it is reached.

head: method
what it does
rows: Records the screen showing now under a name, with the regions that identify it and its named areas. Needs the program stopped.
Says where the program keeps its own mouse pointer, so a move can be checked against it. Works while the program runs.
Reads a map file; nothing is written to disk. Works while the program runs.
Writes the loaded map and the screens added since as one file, which becomes the loaded map. Works while the program runs.

arguments.screen: For `add`: the name the screen is recorded under.
arguments.match: For `add`: 1 to 16 rectangles `[x, y, width, height]` that always look the same on this screen. They are what identifies it.
arguments.controls: For `add`: the screen's named areas, each `{"name", "rect"}`. Left out, none.
arguments.cells: For `add`: `index` compares palette indices, not the colours shown, so one map serves a program shown through two palettes. Left out, `rgb`.
arguments.anchor: For `add`: a symbol or an address the program reaches once the screen is fully drawn. `run_to(screen=)` runs to it.
arguments.path: For `load`: the map file, named `<application>-screen-map.json`, as an absolute or `~`-led path.
arguments.scale: For `load`: how many times larger this machine shows the program's picture, 1 to 8. Left out, 1.
arguments.margin: For `load`: `[x, y]`, the border in machine pixels on each side of the program's picture. Left out, none.
arguments.dest: For `save`: the file to write, named `<application>-screen-map.json`, as an absolute or `~`-led path.
arguments.overwrite: For `save`: `true` replaces a file already at `dest`. Left out, an existing file is refused.
arguments.pointer: For `pointer`: `{"x": ref, "y": ref, "bytes": 2}`, a symbol or a `SEG:OFF` address for each axis. `bytes` is 1, 2 or 4; left out, 2.

returns.match: `add`: each region as recorded, with its `crop` and its `signature`, the fingerprint taken from the screen.
returns.replaced: `add`: `true` when a screen of that name was already added this session. `shadows_file` is `true` when the loaded file has one too.
returns.kept: `add`: reads `N saved for promote` once the map is a candidate that `promote` can write into your repository's `.scry/` folder.
returns.screens: `load` and `save`: how many screens the map holds; `controls` counts their named areas.
returns.mode: `load` and `save`: `verified` when a screen is checked each time it is reached, `consolidated` when it is trusted without a check.
returns.promoted: `save`: the names of the screens added this session that the file now holds.

refuses: An argument the method does not take.
A name, rectangle, area, pointer or file that is not well formed, or a rectangle outside the screen (`bad_argument`).
An `add` without `anchor` when the loaded map is `consolidated`, or a `save` of one holding a screen with none (`bad_argument`).
A `pointer` on a map loaded with a `scale` or a `margin` (`bad_argument`).
`cells` `index` in a mode with no palette (15-, 16- or 32-bit colour), or a video mode `screen_view` cannot read (`no_channel`).
A `save` with nothing mapped and no pointer (`needs_call`).
why: A screen is recognised by a few regions that never change, not by the whole picture: a cursor or a moving ball would change a fingerprint of the whole screen.

The map has two layers. Screens you `add` live in the session and win over a loaded file's screen of the same name; `save` writes both as one file. A new `start` empties the session layer and keeps the file.

A map's `mode` says who keeps it true. In a `verified` map, `run_to(screen=)` checks the screen's regions on reaching it and refuses a map that no longer matches (`stale_map`). In a `consolidated` map the screen is trusted at its `anchor`, which lets one map serve two versions of a program whose pixels differ.
why_more: The mode is the file's own: `save` keeps the loaded map's, and writes `verified` when none was loaded. `screen_map_find` checks the regions in either mode.

Rectangles are in the program's units: character cells in a text mode, pixels in a graphics mode. With `scale` and `margin`, this machine's picture is the program's size times the scale, plus the margin on each side. A read is sampled back to the program's size before it is compared.
A map file is kept in the program's repository, as `.scry/maps/<application>-screen-map.json`, and looks like this.

```json
{"format": "scry-screen-map/1", "application": "bricks", "mode": "verified",
 "screens": [{"name": "play", "kind": "pixel", "size": [320, 200], "anchor": "main_loop",
              "match": [{"crop": [0, 0, 52, 8], "signature": "<16 hex>"}],
              "controls": [{"name": "court", "rect": [200, 80, 80, 40]}]}]}
```

A program that keeps a mouse pointer of its own and clamps it drifts from the mouse driver's. With `pointer` given, `send_mouse` reads the program's pointer back and corrects until it is where it was asked to be. A `save` keeps the pointer, and a `load` replaces it.

In the replay test `perform_export` writes, `load` and `add` are replayed as steps and `screen_map_find` becomes a check of what it matched. A `save` is left out, since a replay would find its file there.

palette.what: Read the colours the palette holds now, as a list and as a picture of colour swatches.

arguments.first: The first entry to read, 0 to 255: an integer or a `0x` string. Left out, 0.
arguments.count: How many entries to read. Left at 0, every entry from `first` to the last.
arguments.scale: The whole factor the picture is enlarged by, 1 to 8. Left at 0, the largest that fits.
arguments.dest: A new path for the PNG, absolute or starting with `~`. Left empty, the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.

returns.colors: Each entry read, as `#rrggbb`, in order from `first`.
returns.rgb: Each entry as the debugger prints it: three six-bit components in hex.
returns.entries: How many entries the palette has: 256.
returns.bits: The width of each component in the DAC, the chip that holds the palette: 6, or the call is refused.
returns.pel_mask: The DAC's pixel mask register, as the debugger prints it.
returns.image: The PNG: its `path`, `bytes`, `sha256`, `width`, `height` and `scale`, whether it is `indexed`, and `inline` or the reason in `not_inlined`.

refuses: An entry past 255, a `scale` outside 0 to 8, or a `dest` that is relative or exists (`bad_argument`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A DAC that is not in six-bit mode (`unexpected_answer`).
A picture the disk could not take whole (`host_failed`).
why: The colours are the VGA DAC's 256 entries, read from the debugger's `VGA DAC` and `VGA DACPAL` listings. Each six-bit component is widened to eight bits as the emulator draws it, by repeating its two top bits below.
The picture is an indexed PNG: every pixel of a swatch holds that entry's index into the DAC, so the file carries the palette as data.
palette.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped once its play screen is drawn. Entries 32 to 39 are colours the game itself sets.
palette.ask: Show me palette entries 32 to 39, and save the swatches as palette.png.
palette.reads: Eight of the palette's 256 entries, from 32, each as `#rrggbb`: the VGA's six-bit components widened to eight bits. The swatches went to a PNG enlarged 8 times, attached to the reply.

screen_view.what: Read the screen at a stop: its text or its picture, the pixels that hold chosen palette indices, the indices in use, or one pixel.

head: mode
what it answers
rows: The screen: its text in a text mode, else a PNG. In a mode drawn through the palette, each pixel of the file is its palette index.
The picture with the palette indices in `pens` in magenta and every other pixel grey, and how many pixels hold them.
No picture: each palette index in use with how many pixels hold it, and the ranges nothing uses.
The palette index and the colour under `point`, with a small picture of the pixels round it.

arguments.pens: For `isolate`: the palette indices to show, 1 to 64 of them. A pen is the palette index a pixel holds.
arguments.point: For `pixel`: the pixel to read, `[x, y]` on the screen.
arguments.crop: The rectangle to read, `[x, y, width, height]`, in characters in a text mode and in pixels otherwise; not for `pixel`. Left out, the whole screen.
arguments.scale: The whole factor the picture is enlarged by, 1 to 8; not for `histogram` or a text mode. Left at 0, the largest that fits.
arguments.dest: A new path for the PNG, absolute or starting with `~`. Left empty, the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.
arguments.attach: `false` writes the picture without attaching it to the reply. Left out, `true`.

returns.text: In a text mode: one string for each row of the crop, as code page 437 draws it, trailing spaces dropped.
returns.cursor: In a text mode: `[column, row]` inside the crop. Unavailable when the cursor is hidden or outside it.
returns.image: In a graphics mode: the PNG: its `path`, `bytes`, `sha256`, `width`, `height` and `scale`, whether it is `indexed`, and `inline` or the reason in `not_inlined`. Not for `histogram`.
returns.pen: For `pixel`: the palette index under the point; `color` is the colour it shows.
returns.histogram: For `histogram`: one `[pen, pixels]` pair for each palette index in use. `pens_used` counts them; `unused` lists the rest as ranges.
returns.pixels: For `isolate`: how many pixels hold the indices asked for. `bbox` is the rectangle that holds them all, as `[left, top, right, bottom]`.

refuses: An argument the mode does not take, or `dest`, `scale` or `attach` in a text mode or with `histogram` (`bad_argument`).
A `crop` or a `point` off the screen, a `scale` outside 0 to 8, or a `dest` that is relative or exists (`bad_argument`).
`isolate`, `histogram` or `pixel` in a text mode or a direct-colour mode, which hold no palette index (`no_channel`).
A video mode it does not read, a split screen or panning, or a build whose debugger has no `VGAMEMDUMP` command for a mode that needs it (`no_channel`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A DAC that is not in six-bit mode (`unexpected_answer`).
why: The screen is read from video memory and never by touching the video card, so reading it does not change it. Text and mode 13h come through the CPU's own view of that memory; planar, unchained and linear modes come from the video RAM, through the debugger's `VGAMEMDUMP` command.

In a mode drawn through the palette, the PNG's pixels are the bytes the program wrote and its palette is the DAC, so the file is data. A 16-colour pixel goes through the Attribute Controller to its DAC entry; a 15- or 16-bit one is widened to eight bits a component by repeating its high bits.
The views by palette index need a mode drawn through the palette: 256 colours, 16-colour planar or 8-bit linear. Nothing says who set a colour, because the debugger does not log writes to the DAC.
why_more: `isolate` draws the other pixels in greys with no black or white. Dimming would lose a dark entry in a dark screen, and one hue over greys stands out whatever the entry's colour.
For `pixel` the picture is a crop of 48 pixels round the point, in colour, with the point ringed and a `border` round the crop. `point_in_crop` is the point inside it.

In protected mode the screen is read through a data segment that covers it: the lowest present one of the GDT, then of the LDT. With paging on, every page must map to the same physical address; otherwise the call is refused (`no_channel`).

A 256-colour picture, each pixel doubled each way as the emulator draws mode 13h, equals the emulator's own capture. A screen that runs past its memory window is refused, and a picture the disk could not take whole is `host_failed`.

`vga_mode` is the video mode as the debugger names it, `kind` is `text` or `pixel`, and `display_start` is where in video memory the screen begins. `screen_indexed` and `entries` come in a graphics mode drawn through the palette.
screen_view.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped once its play screen is drawn.
screen_view.ask: Show me the screen as it is now and save the picture as wall.png.
screen_view.reads: The screen is in the 256-colour mode the debugger names `M_VGA`, 320x200, drawn through a palette of 256 entries (`screen_indexed`). The PNG is enlarged 4 times, to 1280x800, and attached.

screen_signature.what: Get a short hash of what the screen shows, so two screens can be told the same without comparing pictures.

arguments.crop: The rectangle to hash, `[x, y, width, height]`, in characters in a text mode and in pixels otherwise. Left out, the whole screen.

returns.signature: 16 hex characters. Two screens, or two crops of one size, show the same when their signatures are equal.
returns.kind: `text` when characters were hashed, `pixel` when pixels were.
returns.vga_mode: The video mode, as the debugger names it.

refuses: A `crop` that leaves the screen (`bad_argument`).
A video mode `screen_view` does not read, or a build whose debugger has no `VGAMEMDUMP` command for a mode that needs it (`no_channel`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A DAC that is not in six-bit mode (`unexpected_answer`).
why: The signature answers "is it the same screen" with two strings, never two pictures. A caller that waits for a screen, compares two moments or keeps a reference holds 16 characters, not a PNG.
It is made of what the program put in video memory and in the palette, not of what the window drew. An unchanged screen has one signature on any computer.
A character counts by its byte and the two colours its attribute gives it, a pixel by its colour. A palette fade or a recoloured character is a new signature; the cursor's blink is not.
why_more: It reads what `screen_view` reads. Each row of a series carries a signature in the same format, which [Media files](../../REFERENCE.md#media-files) sets out.
The signature is BLAKE2b with an 8-byte digest, written as 16 lowercase hex characters. It hashes `scry-sig/1|<kind>|<w>x<h>|` and then the crop's cells, row by row, `w` and `h` being the crop's.

A text cell is its code page 437 byte, then its foreground and background colours as the VGA shows them. Each goes through the Attribute Controller's palette registers (`VGA AC`), then the DAC. When `mode_control` bit 7 is set, `color-select` supplies bits 5 and 4 in place of the register's. With blinking on, `mode_control` bit 3, the background has three bits and the fourth blinks.
screen_signature.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped once its play screen is drawn. The rectangle is the word SCORE at the top left.
screen_signature.ask: Give me the signature of the SCORE label, the 52 by 8 pixels at the top left of the screen.
screen_signature.reads: `f38d22147fd6e2bd` stands for those 52x8 pixels, hashed by colour (`kind` `pixel`). While the label stays unchanged, the same rectangle gives the same 16 characters.

scan.what: Find the byte that holds a value nobody has named: start from a whole range and keep only what changes as the value does.
scan.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen with its symbols loaded. The example session filters after its first brick falls, when the score reads 60.
scan.ask: Find the byte that holds the score: scan the 216 bytes from row_colours, and filter once a brick has fallen.

then.lead: Then, with the score at 60 after the first brick:

scan.reads: Of 216 bytes, two hold 60 (`0x3c`). One of them, `08DF:00000615`, is where `read_memory` finds the symbol `score`.

head: method
what it does
rows: Opens a scan: every cell of the range is a candidate.
Keeps the candidates whose value passes a comparison.

arguments.ref: Where the range begins, for `start`: a `SEG:OFF` address or a symbol.
arguments.length: How many bytes to scan, for `start`: at most `0xFFFFFF`, and a whole number of candidates.
arguments.cell_bytes: The size of each candidate: 1, 2 or 4 bytes, low byte first. Left out, one byte.
arguments.operator: The comparison a `filter` makes. Left out, `=`.
arguments.value: What each candidate is compared with: an integer or a `0x` string. Left out, what it held at `start`.
arguments.limit: How many of the candidates left the reply lists: 1 to 400. Left out, 40.

returns.hits: The first `limit` of them, each with its address and its value now. None are listed while more than 400 are left.
returns.iterations: How many filters this scan has taken.
returns.closed: `true` when a filter left no candidate, which ends the scan.
returns.truncated: `true` when there are more candidates than `hits` lists.

refuses: An argument the method does not take.
A second `start` while a scan is open, or a `filter` with none (`needs_call`).
A `value` wider than the scan's candidates (`bad_argument`).
A range that runs past the memory the debugger addresses (`bad_argument`).
why: The candidates live in the debugger's own value scanner, `MEMFIND`, not in the reply. So a scan over a large range costs one command, and the addresses are listed only once few enough are left.
That scanner holds one scan at a time, which is why a second `start` is refused until you `clear`.
Without a `value`, a filter compares each candidate with what it held at `start`: `!` keeps the ones that changed, `>` the ones that grew. A few rounds leave the one address.

set_register.what: Force a register to a value you choose, and see what the cpu holds afterwards.
set_register.ask: Set AX to 0, so the game takes this brick for one of the top row.
set_register.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped at `brick_hit` as the ball knocks out its first brick. AL holds the brick's row there.
set_register.reads: AX now holds 0. `readback` is what the register held after the write, four digits for a 16-bit name, and `verified` says it equals what was asked.

arguments.name: The register, as the debugger's `SR` command takes it: a 32-bit one (`eax`), a segment (`ds`), or a 16-bit low half (`ax`, `ip`).
arguments.value: The value to set: an integer or a `0x` string, not negative and no wider than the register.

returns.register: The register written, in lower case.
returns.value: What was asked, as `0x` text at the register's width.
returns.readback: What the register holds after the write, in the same spelling. A 16-bit name is read as the low half of its 32-bit register, so four digits.
returns.regs: Every register as it reads after the write.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A name the debugger does not set; the message lists the ones it does (`bad_argument`).
A negative value, or one wider than the register, before anything is sent (`bad_argument`).
Registers that do not come back after the write, so it cannot be read back (`readback_refused`).
why: The value is read back because a register can refuse part of it. `verified: false` is not always a failure: a register that masks the value is doing its job.
The write marks the session: the `session` block of every later reply carries `altered`, which says this session has written to the machine.

write.what: Write bytes into memory at an address or a symbol, and see what the memory holds afterwards.
write.ask: Set the game's quit flag, so it exits by itself.
write.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, at any stop, with its symbols loaded: `quit` is the flag the game checks to leave.
write.reads: The byte at `08DF:00000619` now holds 1. `readback` is what the memory holds after the write, and `verified` says it is what was sent.

arguments.ref: Where the bytes go: a `SEG:OFF` address or a symbol.
arguments.data_hex: The bytes to write, as hex digits, two per byte: 1 to 128 bytes, what one read takes back for the readback.

returns.readback: The bytes at the address after the write, as hex.
returns.bytes_written: How many bytes were sent, whether or not they landed.
returns.seg_off: The address `ref` resolved to, as segment and offset.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
`data_hex` that is not whole hex bytes, is empty, or holds more than 128 (`bad_argument`).
A real-mode address in ROM, before anything is sent (`bad_argument`).
Bytes that run past what an offset can reach in the cpu's mode (`bad_argument`).
A symbol the loaded table lacks (`unknown_ref`), or one it holds twice (`ambiguous_ref`).
why: `verified: false` on RAM means the write went nowhere; on a hardware register it can be the register answering something else, which is its job.
ROM is refused because `SM`, the debugger's memory-write command, ends the emulator there instead of writing.
The write marks the session: the `session` block of every later reply carries `altered`, which says this session has written to the machine.

debug.what: Send one command to the debugger and read what it printed, for what no other tool does.
debug.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, at any stop.
debug.reads: `output` holds what the debugger's `FPU` command printed, shown here cut short: the whole reply below has it all. No other tool reads the FPU's registers.

arguments.command: One debugger command, as you would type it at the debugger's command line.

returns.output: What the debugger printed. Past 4000 characters it is cut: `clipped` is `true` and `output_path` names a file with all `output_chars` of it.
returns.note: Set when the debugger did not take the command: it does not know it, or refused it for the reason `output` shows.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A command that lets the program run: `RUN`, `VRT`, `RUNWATCH`, `INT`, `STEPIN`, `LOG` and its family. The message names the tool to use (`bad_argument`).
A control character, such as a line break (`bad_argument`).
`DOSTRACE` with a file or `OFF`, which would move or end the trace the `dos` log reads (`bad_argument`).
why: A command that lets the program run is refused before it is sent. It would leave the debugger without the session knowing, and `status` and `last_stop` would go on naming the stop before it. A line break would carry a second command past that check.
A command that writes to the machine, such as `SM` or `LOADSTATE`, marks the session: every later reply carries `altered` in its `session` block.

port.what: Read or write one I/O port, and be told when no device answers there.
port.ask: Read VGA port 3C8h, the index of the next palette entry to be written.
port.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen.
port.reads: Port `0x3C8` reads `0x28`, an 8-bit value: the next palette entry to be written is 40.

head: method
what it does
rows: Reads the port and returns its `value`. Takes `port` and `bits`.
Sends `value` to the port. Takes `port`, `value` and `bits`.

arguments.port: The port: an integer or `0x` hex, 0 to `0xFFFF`.
arguments.bits: The size of the access: 8, 16 or 32 bits. Left out, 8.
arguments.value: What a `write` sends: an integer or `0x` hex, no wider than `bits`.

returns.value: What the read returned, or what the write sent, as `0x` text at the width of `bits`.
returns.port: The port, as four hex digits.
returns.readback: On a `write`: always unavailable, `available: false` with its `why`, because a port holds no value to read back.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A port past `0xFFFF`, a value wider than `bits`, or an argument the method does not take (`bad_argument`).
A port no device answers at that size and direction (`no_channel`).
A DOSBox-X whose debugger has no `PORTINFO` command (`no_channel`).
A debugger answer in a shape the tool does not know (`unexpected_answer`).
why: The debugger's `PORTINFO` is asked before every access, because a port with no device reads all ones and takes a write in silence: nothing in the value says so.
It reports each width apart, and an access the emulator splits byte by byte reaches a device only if every byte does. So a 16-bit read of `0x3DA` is refused where an 8-bit one answers.
A read marks the session `altered` too: reading a port is a bus cycle the device sees.

pic.what: Read the 8259 interrupt controllers, or mask, unmask, acknowledge, raise or lower one interrupt line.
pic.ask: Which interrupt lines are masked right now?
pic.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen.
pic.reads: Two controllers, with lines 3, 5, 6, 7, 10 and 11 masked and none requested. The whole reply below has a row for each controller and each line.

head: method
what it does
rows: Lists the controllers and every line. It writes nothing.
Clears the in-service bit of line `irq`.

arguments.method: `read`, or one of the five actions above.
arguments.irq: The interrupt line an action works on, 0 to 15; 8 to 15 are on the slave controller. `read` takes none.

returns.controllers: On `read`: one row per `controller`, `master` then `slave`, with its `vector_base`, its `active_irq` and the registers `isr` and `isrr`.
returns.irqs: On `read`: one row per line, with `irq`, `vector`, and whether it is `requested`, `masked` and `in_service`. `cascade` marks the line that links the two controllers.
returns.line: After an action: the row of that line as it reads now, with the keys of an `irqs` row.
returns.method: After an action: the action taken, with `irq` the line.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
An `irq` outside 0 to 15, or on a slave controller this machine does not have (`bad_argument`).
An argument the method does not take (`bad_argument`).
A DOSBox-X whose debugger has no `PIC` command (`no_channel`).
A `mask` or `unmask` the listing does not show afterwards (`readback_refused`).
A listing in a shape the tool does not know (`unexpected_answer`).
why: The debugger takes any line number and acts on none past 15, so `irq` is checked before anything is sent.
Only a mask is read back. A raised line on an unmasked input may already have been taken by the cpu when the listing is read, so `line` says what the line holds afterwards.
A controller's `active_irq` is its own line in service, 0 to 7. With none it is unavailable: the emulator writes 8 there, which would read as a ninth line.
why_more: Every action marks the session `altered`, which says this session has written to the machine. A `read` does not.

The `controllers` rows also carry `icw_index`, `icw_words`, `special`, `auto_eoi`, `rotate_eoi`, `single`, `request_issr` and `isr_ignore`: the rest of the 8259's state, named as the debugger's `PIC` listing prints it.

a20.what: Read or set the A20 line, which decides whether addresses past 1 MB wrap around to 0.
a20.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen.
a20.reads: `enabled` is true: the A20 line is on, so addresses past 1 MB do not wrap to 0.

head: method
what it does
rows: Says whether the line is on. It writes nothing.
Turns the line on and reads it back. That is a write: the session is marked `altered`.
Turns the line off, the same way.

returns.enabled: `true` when the A20 line is on.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A DOSBox-X whose debugger has no `A20` command (`no_channel`).
A line that does not read back as set (`readback_refused`).
An answer in a shape the tool does not know (`unexpected_answer`).
why: A DOS kernel loaded into the high memory area turns the line on for itself at each INT 21h. So a line set off may be undone at the program's next DOS call.

run_to.what: Run until the program reaches an address, or a screen of the screen map, and stop there.
run_to.ask: Run until the ball hits a brick, and check that the game's retrace wait keeps running meanwhile.
run_to.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen with its symbols loaded.
