run_to.reads: The run reached `brick_hit`, which is what `TARGET` says. The control `retrace` ran 34 times on the way, so breakpoints were firing, and both breakpoints of the run are removed.

arguments.ref: The address to stop at: a loaded symbol or a hex `SEG:OFF`. Give this or `screen`, never both.
arguments.control: An address known to run often, counted beside the target, so that "the target never ran" can be told from "nothing ran". Required with `ref` or an anchored `screen`.
arguments.screen: A screen of the loaded screen map, the file naming a program's screens. With an `anchor`, an address the map gives it, the run goes there; without, frame by frame.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the stop, in real seconds, before the server interrupts the machine. Left out, 30.
arguments.disarm_watches: `true` takes your watches off for this run, so none of them stops it, and sets them again at the end.

returns.verdict: How the run ended: `TARGET`, the target was reached; `TIMEOUT`, the wait gave up; `OTHER_STOP`, a breakpoint or a watch nobody targeted stopped it first.
returns.control_hits: How many times the controls ran during the run. A `TARGET` is `ok` even with none.
returns.controls: One row per control counted: its `ref`, `at` (where the debugger set it), `hits_in_run` and `removed`. It comes with a run to a `ref` or an anchor.
returns.target_disarmed: Whether the run's own breakpoint at the target was removed.
returns.frames: How many frames a run to a screen with no `anchor` took.
returns.screen: After a run to a screen: its `screen`, `layer` and `mode`, and `judged`, whether the map checked the screen there.

refuses: A `ref` or a `control` that no loaded symbol table holds, or a `screen` the map does not name (`unknown_ref`).
A name that several symbols share (`ambiguous_ref`).
No `control` with a `ref` or an anchored screen, or a `control` or `disarm_watches` with a screen that has no anchor (`bad_argument`).
A control at the target's address (`bad_argument`).
A breakpoint the debugger does not list after being told to set it, found before the machine moves (`readback_refused`).
A `TIMEOUT` during which no control ran: nothing was learned about the target (`control_silent`).
Another stop before any control ran (`cut_by_other_stop`).
A machine that did not report stopped after the interrupt at the time limit (`not_settled`).
A screen map that no longer matches the screen at its anchor (`stale_map`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: A breakpoint can stay silent for reasons that have nothing to do with the program, as one set in ROM does. That looks exactly like "that routine is never called". The control counting beside the target tells them apart, so a `TIMEOUT` with no control hit is refused: it proves nothing about the target.

The target is a temporary breakpoint of the run's own, removed however the run ends. The debugger's breakpoints are persistent, so one left behind would stop the next `resume` at an address none of your breakpoints names. `target` is that breakpoint as the debugger lists it.
`disarm_watches` is for a watch on a byte written every frame, which would otherwise stop every later run.
why_more: A dynamic cpu core runs its recompiled blocks past a code breakpoint without checking it, so a run there could miss its target and read as "never reached". `start`, `run_to` and `breakpoint_at` say so in `note` when the conf's `[cpu] core=` or a `-set "cpu core=..."` flag selects it.

That `note` names the way out, `start(flags=["-set", "cpu core=normal"])`. `auto` is noted by `run_to` and `breakpoint_at` too, because its protected-mode code runs on the dynamic core. `normal` is not noted.

A control stops the machine at each hit, and the server counts it and resumes. Pick a control that runs a few times during the run: each hit costs a stop and a resume. `control_silent` and `cut_by_other_stop` still carry the stop's readings.

With `disarm_watches` the watches are removed from the debugger for the run and set again at its stop. Their addresses are worked out afresh, so a watch on a pointer that moved follows it. One that cannot be set there waits for the next stop, and `not_rearmed` names it with `why`.

- `disarmed_watches` lists, by `ref`, the watches taken off for the run.
- If the call fails with no reply, what it took off is set again or left waiting. The next stop's `applied_on_stop` says when.
- A watch the debugger kept in spite of the removal is named in `note`, since it could still stop the run.

run_for.what: Run for a number of frames or milliseconds of emulated time and come back stopped.
run_for.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, stopped at `brick_hit` in the middle of a game.
run_for.reads: `ELAPSED` says the three frames ran out as asked. The frame counter went from 244 to 247 in three stops at the retrace, and the cpu spent 68499 cycles.

arguments.milliseconds: How much emulated time to run, in milliseconds. Give this or `frames`, never both.
arguments.frames: How many frames to run, each counted at the screen's vertical retrace. Give this or `milliseconds`, never both.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the run to end, in real seconds. Left out, 30.
arguments.disarm_watches: `true` takes your watches off for this run, so none of them stops it, and sets them again at the end.

returns.verdict: How the run ended: `ELAPSED`, the frames or time asked for ran out, as asked; `TIMEOUT`, the wait gave up; `OTHER_STOP`, a breakpoint or a watch stopped it first.
returns.frame_after: The frame counter after the run; `frame_before` is the one before. Unavailable, with why, when `RUNSTATE` prints no frame count.
returns.emulated_after_s: The emulated clock after the run, in seconds; `emulated_before_s` is the one before.
returns.cycles: The cpu cycles the run took. A count only on a session started on the `normal` cpu core; otherwise unavailable, with why.
returns.polls: How many retraces the run stopped at.
returns.retrace_pending: `true` when a stop at the next retrace is still armed in the debugger, so the next resume stops there.

refuses: Both `milliseconds` and `frames` above zero, or neither, or a negative one (`bad_argument`).
A run during which the emulated clock did not move (`no_progress`).
`milliseconds` when `RUNSTATE` gave no clock to count from; nothing ran (`unexpected_answer`).
A DOSBox-X whose debugger has no `RUNSTATE` command (`no_channel`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: The run is the debugger's `VRT` command, once per frame. By `milliseconds` it still ends on a retrace, the first at or past the time asked, so it can run over by up to one frame. A stop between two retraces is not one a replay could reach again.

A breakpoint that stops the run in the middle of a frame leaves that frame's retrace stop armed in the debugger. The reply is `OTHER_STOP` with `retrace_pending: true`, and the next resume stops at the next retrace. The first later stop that none of your breakpoints explains names that retrace as the likeliest cause.

An `ELAPSED` run of N frames, with nothing else able to stop the machine, moves `frame` by exactly N. On a dynamic cpu core a code breakpoint set after its code already ran can fail to stop the frames after it. So `ELAPSED` there does not prove its address was not reached, which `note` says.
why_more:
- The stop of a change watch or an interrupt breakpoint cannot be told from a retrace, so it counts as a frame. `note` says when one is set.
- A `TIMEOUT` whose `VRT` is still running is interrupted where it stands, with its retrace left pending.
- `note` states what the reply cannot prove: a breakpoint or a watch that is set, a clock that could not be read.
- A run does not mark the session `altered`.
- The call reports progress to the client while it waits.

trace.what: Run a number of instructions with the debugger's CPU log on and get every address executed, grouped by symbol.
trace.ask: Trace the next 40 instructions and tell me which routines they run through.
trace.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, stopped inside `brick_hit`. It needs a DOSBox-X built with heavy debugging, started on the `normal` cpu core.
trace.reads: All 40 instructions ran, which is what `ELAPSED` says, at 34 distinct addresses. `trace`, in the whole reply, lists the routines they ran through.

head: shape
the debugger command it uses
rows: `LOGL`, whose lines say their own cpu mode.

arguments.instructions: How many instructions to run and log.
arguments.shape: Which of the debugger's log formats to write, as above. Left out, `normal`.
arguments.dest: Where the log ends up: an absolute or `~` path to a new file in a folder that exists. Left empty, the next `trace-<n>.trace` among the captures.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the log to finish, in real seconds. Left out, 60.

returns.verdict: `ELAPSED`, every instruction ran; `OTHER_STOP`, a breakpoint or a pending retrace stopped it first; `TIMEOUT`, the wait gave up and the run was interrupted where it stood.
returns.trace: The result: `path` to the log, `set_path` to the list of addresses, `instructions` executed, distinct `addresses`, `unplaced` (addresses no symbol covers) and `symbols`.

refuses: A DOSBox-X built without heavy debugging, which `build_check` reports as `heavy_debug` (`no_channel`).
A working directory the emulator cannot write, since the debugger opens its log there (`no_channel`).
A `LOGCPU.TXT` already in the emulator's working directory: it is somebody's, so move it aside; it is never deleted (`bad_argument`).
A cpu core whose cycle count does not move one per instruction: `start(flags=["-set", "cpu core=normal"])` (`no_channel`).
A log the machine closed before the trace stopped, an empty log, or one that would not close (`readback_refused`).
A log file the debugger could not create; nothing ran (`host_failed`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: The debugger's log ends with the instruction it stops at, logged and not executed, so a complete file holds one line more than `instructions`. A trace runs forward only. The debugger writes its history of what ran before a stop only when the emulator exits, so that question is a trace from an earlier stop.

A trace checks its own count. A line is one executed instruction only on the `normal` cpu core, so the cycle count `RUNSTATE` gives must have moved by the lines the file holds. That is why any other core is refused.
The debugger writes its log only in the emulator's working directory, so the file passes through there on its way to `dest`.
why_more:
| in `trace` | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `path`, `bytes`, `shape` | the log, its size and its format |
| `set_path` | a file with one JSON line per executed address: `seg_off`, `addr` and `symbol` with `delta` where they can be worked out, `count`. Unavailable when it could not be written, which `note` says |
| `instructions`, `addresses`, `unplaced` | instructions executed, distinct addresses, addresses no symbol covers |
| `symbols` | the first rows, by address: `symbol`, `addr`, `addresses`, `instructions`, `first`, `last` |
| `symbols_total`, `truncated` | how many symbols ran, and whether `symbols` leaves some out |
| `closed` | on a refusal: whether the log was closed |

An interrupt breakpoint stops inside its `INT`, after the counter took it and before it ran, so a run it stops may count one more than it executed. The log writes each line before breakpoints are checked, so a trace started on a breakpoint's address stops there again with nothing executed.

The machine can close the log itself: the BIOS's power-on self test does, so a trace started right after a reset meets it. How each address gets its symbol is in [REFERENCE.md](../../REFERENCE.md#a-trace-says-which-routines-ran).
How a logged address becomes a linear one, and so gets its symbol:

- In real or virtual-8086 mode it is `CS` times 16 plus `EIP`. Otherwise it is the base of the selector in `CS` plus `EIP`.
- That selector counts only as a present code descriptor whose privilege is the one it requests, read from one `GDT` and `LDT` listing at the stop.
- A trace that starts and stops in real mode is read the real-mode way, even where it passed through protected mode.
- An address with no linear form gets no symbol, and counts in `unplaced`.

screen_wait.what: Run until the screen shows a text, a mapped screen, a black palette or a change of screen, and stop there.
screen_wait.ask: Run until the game's play screen is up.
screen_wait.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, right after `start`, with the game's screen map loaded.
screen_wait.reads: The map's `play` screen was not up at the call, which is `already: false`. It came up 2 frames later, and the machine stopped there.

arguments.text: Wait until this text is on the text screen: 1 to 132 characters of code page 437, matched exactly, case included, inside one row.
arguments.screen: Wait until this screen of the loaded screen map, the file naming a program's screens, is the one shown.
arguments.palette: `black` waits until every palette entry is black, which is how a fade ends.
arguments.changed: `true` waits until the screen map names a different screen from the one it named at the start. A frame it cannot name counts as in between.
arguments.every: How many frames to run between two looks at the screen. Left at 0, every frame; a screen shown for fewer frames than this can be missed.
arguments.on_breakpoint: Look at the screen only at the end of a frame in which this breakpoint fired: its `ref`, as `declaration_list` lists it.
arguments.on_watch: The same for a watch: the `ref` of a `change` watch you set.
arguments.condition: Counts only the firings where this holds. Up to four terms joined by `&&`, each a register or a memory read (`b@ref`, `w@ref`, `d@ref`) compared with a hex value.
arguments.seconds: How long to keep looking, in real seconds, counted from the first look. Left out, 30.

returns.verdict: `TARGET` when what you waited for is on screen. `TIMEOUT` when the wait gave up, with a `note` and the machine stopped.
returns.already: `true` when it was on screen at the call, so the machine did not move.
returns.predicate: Which of `text`, `screen`, `palette` or `changed` was waited on.
returns.point: With `text`: where it was found, as `[column, row]`. `line` is that row's whole text.
returns.screen: The screen found, as `name` and `layer`. With `changed`, `started_on` is the screen it replaced.

refuses: None or several of `text`, `screen`, `palette` and `changed` (`bad_argument`).
A screen the map does not name, or a breakpoint or watch you did not set (`unknown_ref`).
`changed` with no screen map loaded (`needs_call`).
A breakpoint or watch that never fired within `seconds`: no screen was looked at (`never_fired`).
A stop nobody asked for that ends the wait early; its `cause` comes with it (`wait_stopped`).
A screen that cannot be read, or a DOSBox-X whose debugger has no `RUNSTATE` command (`no_channel`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: The wait runs the machine one frame at a time, to each vertical retrace, and looks at the screen there. Each look costs a stop and a read, so for a screen that is far away use `run_for` first.

`seconds` is counted from after the first read so that a short one still reaches the first frame; a frame read under way when it passes is finished. A wait that gives up never leaves the machine running: a `VRT` still running is interrupted where it stands.

If what you wait for is already on screen the reply comes at once and the machine does not move. Under `on_breakpoint` or `on_watch` the first firing is awaited even so. With `text`, a frame that is not in a text mode is no match.
why_more:
- `waited_on` repeats what was waited on: its `kind`, its `ref`, and the `condition` if any.
- Under `on_breakpoint` or `on_watch`, `firings` and `frames_examined` (the frames looked at after a firing) replace `polls` and `sampled_every`, in refusals too.
- `fired_line` is unavailable here, with why: the debugger reports no screen line at a stop.
- `palette` and `entries` come with a black palette: the value asked for, and how many palette entries were read.
- On a `TIMEOUT`, `text` holds the rows of the last text screen read, and `retrace_pending` says whether a retrace stop is still armed.
- A `note` on a `TARGET` means a watch or an interrupt breakpoint is set whose stop the wait could have taken for a retrace.
- A refusal after the machine ran carries `polls` and `stop_seq`. `wait_stopped` adds `retrace_pending` and `text`.
- `enrichment` comes where `stop_seq` was due and the stop could not be read.

step.what: Execute a few instructions, going into calls or over them.
step.ask: Execute two instructions and show me where the program is now.
step.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, stopped at `brick_hit`, where the `run_to` example above ends.
step.reads: Both instructions ran, from `08DF:000002C8` to `08DF:000002CC`. `stalled: 0` says neither of them left the address unchanged.

head: mode
what it does
rows: Executes one instruction, and enters a call.
Runs a `CALL`, an `INT`, a `LOOP` or a `REP` to the next instruction as one step.

arguments.count: How many instructions to execute. Left out, one.

returns.instructions_completed: How many instructions ran. Fewer than `asked` when an `over` did not come back and the remaining steps were not sent.
returns.before: Where the machine was before the steps, as `SEG:OFF`; `after` is where it is now.
returns.moved: `false` when no step changed the address.
returns.stalled: How many steps left the address unchanged: an iteration of a `rep`, a jump to itself or a halt.

refuses: `over` on a DOSBox-X whose debugger has no `RUNSTATE` command (`no_channel`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: `into` is the debugger's own `STEPIN`. `over` is built from several commands: a breakpoint on the next instruction, a run, a wait for the stop, and the breakpoint removed. That wait is why `over` needs `RUNSTATE`.

An `over` that has not come back within its time limit is interrupted where it stands, and the remaining steps are not sent. A machine that could not be stopped is left running, which `session.running` says. `note` appears when the step's own breakpoint could not be confirmed removed.

`stalled` is counted step by step, because comparing only the two ends would read a two-instruction loop as a step that went nowhere. The largest `count` limits cost, not risk: past it the tool to use is `run_to`.

resume.what: Let the machine run, either with no deadline or waiting a while for it to stop.
resume.ask: Let the game run until the score changes, for a minute at most.
resume.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, stopped inside `brick_hit`, with a `change` watch set on `score`.
resume.reads: `OTHER_STOP` says something stopped the machine before the minute ran out: here the watch on the score, at `08DF:000002EB` in frame 36.

arguments.seconds: How long to wait for a stop, in real seconds. Left at 0, the call returns at once and the machine keeps running.
arguments.detail: `true` adds `output`, the end of what the debugger printed for its `RUN` command. Left out, `omitted` names the fields not sent.

returns.verdict: With `seconds`: `OTHER_STOP`, a breakpoint or a watch stopped the machine, and the stop's readings follow; `TIMEOUT`, nothing did, and it is left running with a `note`.
returns.waited_s: With `seconds`: how long the call waited.
returns.output: With `detail`: the end of the debugger's own text. `output_chars` is its whole length and `clipped` says whether it was cut.
returns.e9: With a stop: the lines the program wrote to port E9, the emulator's debug output port, since the previous stop. They come with or without `detail`.

refuses: A machine that is already running (`not_stopped`).
`seconds` above 0 on a DOSBox-X whose debugger has no `RUNSTATE` command (`no_channel`).
why: A machine that is already running is refused, because the debugger's `RUN` does nothing there and an `ok` would read as if it had been resumed. No breakpoint has to be set first: `stop` brings a running machine back.

With `seconds` at 0 the call returns straight after resuming and does not look for a stop, so a machine that stops at once is found by the next call. With `seconds`, such a stop is this call's `OTHER_STOP`, and the call reports progress while it waits.

A conf whose autoexec runs `boot` stops once more on its own. `boot` restarts the machine at the boot sector, `0000:7C00`, and the break at every start that `start` asks the debugger for fires there too. `cause` names it, and a second `resume` lets the operating system run.
why_more: On a DOSBox-X whose debugger has no `RUNSTATE` command no reply can see that stop at the boot sector. `stop` brings the machine back from wherever it is, and its position shows it is still there.

wait.what: Let a running program play for a while and see where it is after, without stopping it.
wait.ask: Let the game play for one more second without stopping it.
wait.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, running after a `resume`.
wait.reads: The second ran out with the game still running. That is the answer a wait is for, so `status` is `ok`.

arguments.seconds: How long to let it run, in real seconds. Left out, 30.

returns.verdict: Only when the machine stopped during the wait: `OTHER_STOP`, a breakpoint or a watch stopped it, and the stop's readings follow.

refuses: A machine that is stopped: `resume` it first (`not_running`).
A DOSBox-X whose debugger has no `RUNSTATE` command (`no_channel`).
why: The wait is deliberate, so running out of `seconds` is the answer and not a failure: the reply is `ok`, with a `note` that the machine is still running. `wait` neither resumes nor stops. `resume` lets a stopped machine run, and `stop` brings a running one back.

stop.what: Stop a running machine where it is and read where it stopped.
stop.ask: Stop the game where it is.
stop.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, running after a `resume`.
stop.reads: `interrupted: true` means this call stopped the machine, through the debugger's own interrupt, which is `via: break`. It landed in real mode; where exactly differs from run to run.

arguments.until: `protected` goes on resuming and interrupting, in short runs, until the machine stops in protected mode. Left empty, it stops where it is.

returns.interrupted: `true` when this call stopped the machine, with the stop's readings. `false` when it was already stopped, with a `note`.
returns.via: `break` when the stop came from this call's own interrupt.
returns.runs_to_protected: With `until`: how many short runs it took. A `note` says so when none ended in protected mode.
returns.cpu_mode: The cpu mode the machine stopped in: `real`, `protected`, `paged` or `VM86`.

refuses: A machine that did not report stopped after the interrupt: ask again (`not_settled`).
why: The interrupt goes through the emulator's own debugger connection, the conf's `[dosbox] mcp_server` setting. It needs no window and no menu, and takes nothing from your screen and keyboard.

The machine stops wherever it is, often outside your program. A DJGPP program spends part of every frame in real-mode BIOS handlers, at `F000:xxxx`, where no symbol of a protected-mode table can be given an address. A breakpoint in your code, set at a stop inside it before resuming, brings the machine back into it, and so does `until="protected"`.
why_more: At a stop outside the program, a breakpoint on a symbol reads `unarmable` when the symbol is in the table and its address cannot be worked out at this instant. It reads `unresolved` when the table does not hold the name. That is a fact about the table, since `symbols_load` adds each table to the ones before.
A `stop` on a machine already stopped answers with that stop as `last_stop`. If `stop` fails as well, `close` then `start`.

breakpoint_at.what: Set a breakpoint at a symbol or an address, to stop there or to count how often the code runs.
breakpoint_at.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped in play with `bricks.sym` loaded.
breakpoint_at.ask: Stop the game the next time a brick is hit.

then.lead: Then let the game run, for a minute at most:

breakpoint_at.reads: The breakpoint is armed at `08DF:02C8`. `OTHER_STOP` means something other than the call's own target stopped the machine: here, `cause` names the breakpoint on `brick_hit`.

arguments.ref: Where to break: a symbol or a `SEG:OFF` address in the code.
arguments.by: How `ref` is read: `symbol` or `address` forces one. Left at `auto`, a ref with a colon is an address and anything else a symbol.
arguments.role: `stop` halts the machine there. `control` never halts a run: every `run_to` counts how often the code runs.

returns.state: `armed` when set, `counted` for a `control`, `pending` while the program runs. The top of the page lists the rest.
returns.entry: The debugger's own row for the breakpoint, once armed.
returns.stored: `true` when the server saved the breakpoint. It is set again at `start` and after `symbols_load`.
returns.already_stored: `true` when the same breakpoint was saved already, so the call changed nothing.
returns.marked: `true` when the symbol carries the linker's mark. Whether a breakpoint there fires is an open question, and `note` says so.

refuses: A name that matches several symbols (`ambiguous_ref`).
An address another saved breakpoint already holds; the message names it (`ambiguous_ref`).
The same `ref` under the other role: clear it first (`bad_argument`).
A `SEG:OFF` that is not hex on both sides of the colon (`bad_argument`).
why: A `control` is for an address you know runs. `run_to` counts it beside its target, so a target never reached can be told from code that never ran.

A DOSBox-X breakpoint always halts, so the debugger holds a control only while a `run_to` counts it: each hit stops the machine, is counted and let go. Between runs nothing is set, so `resume`, `run_for` and a wait never stop there.

A symbol missing from the loaded symbol table is saved `unresolved`, not refused: the compiler may have inlined it this time. A raw `SEG:OFF` belongs to the build it was declared over and goes `stale` over another.
why_more:
- A breakpoint at a ROM address is accepted and never fires, while the same command at a RAM address does. Nothing detects it in advance.
- When a `run_to` does not reach such a target, its note names this cause.
- On a dynamic cpu core, or `core=auto` once protected-mode code runs, execution can pass over a breakpoint inside a compiled block. `note` says so.
- A raw `SEG:OFF` declared before any symbol table was loaded is set again at `start`. One declared over a map is set again after a `symbols_load` of the same map.
- `run_to`'s own `control` counts for that run alone: saved as one, it would stop the machine once per hit on every later run.
- An `on_breakpoint` wait on a control is refused.
- Setting needs the machine stopped, and the row is read back from the debugger's list.
- A `pending` one is set by the first call that meets the next stop, a reader such as `registers` included. That call's reply lists it in `applied_on_stop`.
- `by` says how the ref was read and `role` which role it has. `armed` is `true` once the debugger holds the row.

breakpoint_interrupt.what: Stop the machine when the program calls an interrupt, optionally only one `ah` function of it.
breakpoint_interrupt.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped in play just after its quit flag was written, so its next pass of the main loop exits.
breakpoint_interrupt.ask: Stop the game when it calls DOS to exit.

then.lead: Then let the game run, for a minute at most:

breakpoint_interrupt.reads: `BPINT 21 AH=4C` is the breakpoint's name, which `declaration_clear` takes. The game then stops at its exit call, and `cause` gives that interrupt breakpoint as the most likely reason.

arguments.number: The interrupt, `0x00` to `0xFF`, as an integer or a `0x` string: `"0x21"` is DOS.
arguments.ah: Stop only when `AH` holds this function number, `0x00` to `0xFF`. Left out, every call of the interrupt stops.
arguments.detail: `true` adds what the debugger printed for the command, as `output`.

returns.ref: The breakpoint's name, such as `BPINT 21 AH=4B`. `declaration_clear` takes it.
returns.armed: `true` once the debugger holds it. `false` while the program runs: it is set at the next stop.
returns.state: `pending`, and only while the program runs.
returns.entry: The debugger's own row for it, once armed.
returns.already_stored: `true` when the same breakpoint was saved already: nothing was stacked.
returns.output: With `detail=True`, the end of what the debugger printed. `output_chars` is its full length, and `clipped` says it was cut.

refuses: A `number` or an `ah` outside `0x00` to `0xFF` (`bad_argument`).
why: It brings a running program back at that interrupt. `stop` brings it back wherever it is, and a key pressed on the host cannot. Set it before `resume`.

It is saved under its `BPINT` text, so `declaration_list` shows it and `declaration_clear(kind="breakpoint")` removes it by `ref`. It is never cleared by the debugger's row number, which would delete whichever row sits there.
Setting the same one again does nothing, checked against the debugger's list. Sent twice, the debugger stacks a second row that a later clear leaves behind as `foreign`.
why_more:
- A DJGPP program can be caught at interrupt `0x31` with `ah=2`.
- `output` comes only from a call that set a new breakpoint: one left `pending` or already armed typed nothing.
- Without `detail`, `omitted` names the fields left out.
- `stored` is `true` once the server saved it.

regpoint_add.what: Stop the machine when a condition on the registers comes true, wherever the program is, to find who puts a value in a register.
regpoint_add.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped inside `brick_hit` with `bricks.sym` loaded.
regpoint_add.ask: Stop as soon as DX holds 3DAh, the VGA status port.

then.lead: Then let the game run, for a minute at most:

regpoint_add.reads: The registerpoint is armed as the debugger's `BPIF DX==3DA`. The game then stops where DX takes that value: `cause` names the registerpoint and the address.

arguments.condition: Up to four terms joined by `&&`. Each is a register (`AX`, `EAX`, `AL`, `CS`, `FLAGS`), a comparison and a hex value: `AX==3B`.

returns.state: `armed` when set, `pending` while the program runs. The top of the page lists the rest.
returns.ref: The condition as the debugger prints it back. `declaration_clear` takes it.
returns.entry: The debugger's own row for the registerpoint, once armed.
returns.already_stored: `true` when the same registerpoint was saved already, so the call changed nothing.
returns.while_running: `true` when the program was running as the call arrived.

refuses: A term that is not a register, a comparison and a hex value (`bad_argument`).
A DOSBox-X whose debugger has no `BPIF` command (`no_channel`).
why: The debugger compiles the terms once and checks them before every instruction. It fires as the condition comes true: one set while it already holds waits until it no longer does, and a resumed machine does not stop again at once.

When the debugger's `RUNSTATE` command names the row that fired, the stop is credited to that registerpoint. Otherwise the stop's `attribution.regpoints_holding` lists the registerpoints whose condition holds, as the likely cause.
A registerpoint has no address, so it is never `stale` and has no `role`. It compares and never assigns.
why_more:
- The comparisons are `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`, and the value may carry `0x`.
- `by` is always `expr`, and `condition` repeats `ref`. `armed` is `true` once the debugger holds the row.

watch_add.what: Keep a variable in view at every stop, stop the machine when it changes, or count every write to it, by name.
watch_add.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped inside `brick_hit` as the first brick falls, with `bricks.sym` loaded.
watch_add.ask: Stop the game when the score changes, and show me where it stopped.

then.lead: Then let the game run, for a minute at most:

watch_add.reads: `OTHER_STOP` is a stop the call did not target, and its `cause` cannot name a watch. `pc` is just past the instruction that wrote the score, and `watches` in the whole reply holds the new value.

head: mode
what it does
stops?
rows: Reads the value at every stop.
Counts every write and which instruction made it.
Logs a row per access, with the screen line being drawn and the time.
Holds the bytes at their value: whatever the program writes is undone.

arguments.ref: What to watch: a symbol, a `SEG:OFF` address, or an address reached through a pointer (`[base]+0x28`, `base->field`).
arguments.length: Total bytes; not needed when `fmt` has a size or the symbol has a type. At most 128 for `show` and `capture`, 16 for `change` and `freeze`, 1024 for `count`.
arguments.fmt: How the bytes read: a scalar (`u8` to `f64`), an array (`u16[8]`), a string (`char[16]`) or a struct (`{x:i16,y:i16}`).
arguments.by: How `ref` is read: `symbol`, `address` or `pointer` forces one; `auto` lets the server choose.
arguments.trigger: For `capture` only: the address whose every write takes a row holding the block at `ref`.
arguments.trigger_type: `w` takes writes. On a `capture`, `r` takes reads of `ref` itself, with no `trigger`, `length` or `fmt`.

returns.state: `armed` when set in the debugger and able to fire, `evaluated` for a `show` watch, `pending` while the program runs. The top of the page lists the rest.
returns.entry: The debugger's own row for the watch, once armed.
returns.stored: The server saved the watch, and sets it again after `symbols_load`.
returns.caveat: A warning: in protected mode a `change` watch can fire when nothing changed.
returns.entries: Every debugger row the watch uses, one per byte, for `change` and `freeze`.
returns.frozen_hex: For `freeze`: the bytes being held, in hex.

refuses: One `ref` declared two ways (`bad_argument`).
A `length` over the mode's maximum (`bad_argument`).
A `count`, `capture` or `freeze` while the program runs (`not_stopped`), or through a pointer.
A `count` or `capture` on a DOSBox-X without the `TAP` debugger command, or a `freeze` on one built without heavy debugging (`no_channel`).
A `freeze` on an offset already frozen (`ambiguous_ref`).
`trigger` on any mode but `capture`, and a write capture without one (`bad_argument`).
A pointer base the symbol table lacks, most likely a stack local (`unknown_ref`).
A name that matches several symbols, or a `change` watch on a byte another watch already holds (`ambiguous_ref`).
why: A `change` watch breaks when memory changes, which is the thing most likely to be misread: a read never fires it, nor does a write storing the value already there. The debugger compares one byte, so a watch arms a row per byte, and that is why its length is capped.
`count` and `capture` exist for what a stop cannot give: every value a variable takes over a stretch, and who wrote each, while the program keeps running.

A `freeze` is the debugger putting each byte back after every instruction, so it holds against the program's own writes. It holds the values of the stop it is declared at, so a saved freeze is never set again by `start` or `symbols_load`.
why_more: On every watch:

- A `show` watch sets nothing: it is a plain read at every stop. A `change` watch is read at every stop too.
- A `change` watch declared while the program runs is `pending`. The first call that meets the next stop sets it, a reader included, and lists it in `applied_on_stop`.
- A watch saved with no record of its session, marked `orphan: true`, is still read at every stop.
- A NaN or infinite `f32` or `f64` reads as the text `nan`, `inf` or `-inf`, which JSON has no number for.
- A region is `memdump`'s job, which is why lengths are limited.
- With `fmt` left at `auto`, a typed symbol reads as its type, else as the widest unsigned scalar that divides `length`. Otherwise `length` is a whole number of `fmt` values.
- `why` gives the reason for a state that sets nothing, and `addr` is where a `count`, `capture` or `freeze` sits.
On `change`:

- Arming reads the CPU mode off the machine: the same `SEG:OFF` is a different byte in each mode, and the mode changes as the program boots.
- The debugger's `BPLM`, a watch on a linear address, is not offered.
- A DPMI program, a DOS program in protected mode, runs paged, so a memory frame belongs to whoever holds it at that instant.
- For the same reason a protected-mode `change` watch fires on the paging host, not on the program. It is armed, and `caveat` says not to trust its firing.
- In real mode a `change` watch is trusted.
- A watch at a raw `SEG:OFF` keeps the CPU mode of the stop that set it. At a stop of the other mode it reads `unarmable` with no value.
- A watch by symbol or through a pointer is resolved at each stop and keeps no mode.
- `command` is the debugger command sent, and `entry` the row as the debugger lists it: `BPM 0040:006C` lists as `BPMEM 0040:006C`.
- A protected-mode row, `BPPM`, lists its offset in eight digits.
Through a pointer:

- The pointer is read as a near pointer in the base's own segment, at the width its type gives (`ptr16{...}`, `ptr32{...}` in the `types` file).
- With no such type it is four bytes in protected mode and two in real mode. A class after the width (`ptr16@CODE`) is accepted and changes nothing.
- A `change` watch moves with its pointer (`moved`, with `from` and `to`) and with the CPU mode: a row armed in the other mode is armed again in this one.
- A null pointer is `null_pointer`, never a watch at address zero.
- `pointer` holds where the pointer was read (`at`, `length`), its `value`, and the `offset` and `field` added.
On `count` and `capture`:

- The debugger's `TAP` records every access the program makes to that memory, a write storing the value already there included. The debugger's own reads and writes are not recorded.
- A `count` adds up each 32-bit word an access touches, by value and by writer, so `total` counts a write that straddles two words twice.
- A capture of writes keeps the block at `ref` as it stood before the write landed; the write's own value is the row's `data`.
- A capture of reads keeps one row per read of `ref` and no block. On code it also sees the instruction fetches of that byte.
- It goes in at a stop, because it replaces the handler of a memory page, which the debugger does between instructions.
- It is set again at `start` and after `symbols_load`, where its `ref` resolves.
- Something that replaces the page's handler later, such as a video mode change, displaces it: it lists `displaced` and sees nothing more until declared again.
- It needs a cpu core that reads memory through the page handlers, so the dynamic core is refused. Under `core=auto` a protected-mode program is already on that core when stopped.
- One set from real mode cannot cover extended memory. For a DPMI or DJGPP program's variables, start on the normal core: `flags=["-set","cpu core=normal"]`.
- The high memory area is refused because its alias follows the A20 line. So is a range that paging splits across pages that are not adjacent.
- Each stop with one saved costs one `TAPLIST`, which writes its rows and tables to disk.
- `tally_id` is the debugger's number for it, and `trigger_addr` where `trigger` resolves.
On `freeze`:

- It does not hold against what is not an instruction the debugger steps: a dynamic core, a DMA transfer. Each stop reads the bytes back and says `holding` or `not_held`.
- The debugger lists a freeze by its offset alone, so a second one at the same offset is refused: the two rows could not be told apart.
- `entries` are those rows, offset and value with no segment. `addr` is where the freeze is.
- A freeze writes to the machine, so the session reads `altered`, which means written to.

declaration_list.what: List the saved breakpoints, registerpoints and watches, each with its state checked against the debugger's own list.
declaration_list.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped after a recording, with three watches saved: one shown at every stop, one counting writes, one capturing reads.
declaration_list.ask: Which breakpoints and watches are set right now?
declaration_list.reads: Three watches are saved, and no breakpoint or registerpoint. `debugger_read` is `true`: the states come from the debugger's own list, read at this stop.

returns.breakpoints: The saved breakpoints, interrupt breakpoints included. Each row has `ref`, `role`, `state` and, once armed, the debugger's `entry`.
returns.regpoints: The saved registerpoints, each with its `condition`, `state` and `entry`.
returns.watches: The saved watches, each with `mode`, `length`, `fmt` and `state`. A `count` or a `capture` adds its tables.
returns.foreign: Debugger rows the server did not set, by kind, as the debugger lists them. They are listed and never deleted.
returns.debugger_read: `false` while the program runs: the states are then the last stop's, which `last_stop` dates.

why: At a stop each state is the debugger's own answer: the call reads its list back. While the program runs the debugger cannot be asked, so the rows carry the last stop's states.
`inherited` is `true` on a row an earlier session saved, since no reply names this session to compare with. Nothing expires: a row another session left stays until it is cleared by its `ref`.
why_more: What a row carries:

- Every row: `ref`, `by` (how the ref is read), `cpu`, `created_at`, `origin` (the session that saved it), `inherited`, `age_s`, `state`, and `why` where the state needs a reason.
- `cpu` is always an object with `available` set to `false` and a `why`: a DOS machine has one cpu.
- A breakpoint adds `role`, `entry` and `marked`. A row with no session recorded adds `orphan: true`.
- A registerpoint adds `condition` and `entry`.
- A watch adds `mode`, `length`, `fmt`, `pointer` for a ref through one, and a `change` watch's `entry`.
- A `count` or a `capture` adds `tally_id`, `addr`, `trigger`, `trigger_addr`, `trigger_type`, `installed` and `total`.
- A `count` adds `values` (each `at`, `raw_hex`, `count`, and `value` or `partial`), `values_total` and `overflow_values`.
- It also adds `writers` (each `pc`, `count`, `symbol`), `writers_total` and `overflow_pcs`.
- A `capture` adds `rows_path`, `rows_kept`, `rows_max`, `overflow_rows` and `first_rows`.
- Each of `first_rows` has `n`, `frame`, `line`, `time_s`, `pc`, `symbol`, `data`, `mask`, and a write capture's `raw_hex` and `block`.
- A `freeze` adds `addr`, `entries`, `frozen_hex` and `bytes`, what the memory holds now.
The states of a `count`, a `capture` and a `freeze`, beside those at the top of the page:

| `state` | what it means |
|---|---|
| `tallied`, `captured` | Installed and recording. |
| `displaced` | The memory page's handler was replaced since, so it sees nothing more. Declare it again. |
| `unlisted` | The debugger's list did not show it or could not be read, as while the program runs. |
| `unarmed` | This session has not set it. |
| `holding`, `not_held` | A freeze whose bytes still are, or no longer are, the frozen ones. |
| `unreadable` | A freeze whose bytes could not be read. `why` says the reason. |
What the tables say:

- A value's `value` is given when one access covered the range whole; otherwise the row is `partial`.
- `data` and `mask` are the 32-bit word that holds the trigger and which of its bytes the access touched. A word written over the trigger and its neighbour shows both.
- `pc` is the instruction that made the access, with `symbol` when a symbol table names it.
- `time_s` is the emulated clock, `line` the screen line being drawn and `frame` the display's frame count.
- `line` is unavailable before the display has timed its first frame, and `frame` on a DOSBox-X whose `TAP` writes only a row's time and line.
- Rows past the limit are counted in `overflow_rows`, values and writers past theirs in `overflow_values` and `overflow_pcs`, so a table that was cut says so.
- A stop's reply adds `since_last_stop`, and `reset` when the total fell, and never the rows or tables. A listing between two stops uses up nothing.

declaration_clear.what: Remove saved breakpoints, registerpoints or watches: one by its `ref`, or every one of a kind.
declaration_clear.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped with the watch on the score that the `watch_add` entry sets.
declaration_clear.ask: Remove the watch on the score.
declaration_clear.reads: The watch on `score` is gone, and `disarmed` lists the two debugger rows it used, one per byte.

arguments.kind: `breakpoint`, `regpoint` or `watch`: what to clear. `breakpoint` covers interrupt breakpoints too.
arguments.ref: The one to clear, as the reply that saved it gave its `ref`. Left empty with `all=True`.
arguments.all: `true` clears every one of `kind`, and takes no `ref`.

returns.declarations_cleared: How many were removed from the saved breakpoints file.
returns.disarmed: The debugger rows removed, as the debugger listed them, checked by reading its list back.
returns.pending_disarm: Debugger rows still to remove: at the next stop while the program runs, or on the next call when a removal failed.

refuses: An empty `ref` without `all`, or both together (`bad_argument`).
A `ref` that matches nothing: the message names the refs saved (`unknown_ref`).
why: It removes only what this server set: a `foreign` row, one typed through `debug`, is never deleted.

The saved breakpoint or watch is removed at once. While the program runs the debugger cannot be asked, so its rows go at the next stop: `pending_disarm` lists them, and that stop's reply confirms it in `applied_on_stop`.
A `SEG:OFF` and a registerpoint's condition match in any spelling. A symbol or an interrupt breakpoint's `BPINT` text must be the exact text the saving reply carried.

state_list.what: List the session's saved states, with what each file says of itself: program, machine, memory and time.
state_list.ask: Which saved states does this session have?
state_list.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, after a state was saved as `third-brick`. The example session gives `start` a `state_dir` of its own.
state_list.reads: The summary counts one state, and `state_dir` is the folder it is in: the `state_dir` given to `start`.

returns.state_dir: The folder the states are in: the `state_dir` given to `start`, or one in the session's temporary folder, which `close` deletes.
returns.states: One row per named `.sav` file: `name`, `path`, `bytes`, `version`, `program`, `machine`, `memory_mb` and `saved_at`. A row that is no state carries a `note`.
returns.working_slot: The emulator's own numbered slot file, as a row of its own because it is not a named state. Unavailable when it has not been written.

why: The list is read from the folder, not from the machine, so it answers while the program runs.

A file that is not a state keeps its row, with a `note` and its values unavailable. So does a `.sav` that is no regular file: a link to nothing, a directory, a FIFO. A `.sav` under a name no `load` reads, such as `Boss_1.sav` where a state is `boss-1`, carries a `note` saying to rename it.

state_write.what: Save the emulated machine to a file under a name, or load a saved one back.
state_write.ask: Save the machine as it is now under the name bricks, without stopping my game.
state_write.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, while the game runs. The demo saves, presses the left arrow, and loads the state back.

then.lead: Then, after the paddle has moved, the load:

state_write.reads: The game was running, so `paused` is true both times: it was stopped for the command and resumed. `program` and `machine` are read off the state's file.

head: method
what it does
rows: Writes the machine to a new file. It never overwrites one.
Replaces the machine with a saved one. Every later reply then carries `altered`: this session has written to the machine.

arguments.name: The state's name, spelled as a file name is: `Boss_1` becomes `boss-1`. At most 64 characters, with at least one letter or digit, and not digits only.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the debugger's answer to the command, in seconds. Left out, 30.

returns.path: The state's file: `<name>.sav` in the state folder.
returns.paused: `true` when the program was running: it was stopped for the command and resumed afterwards.
returns.program: The program the state was saved from, read off the file with `version`, `machine`, `memory_mb` and `saved_at`.
returns.bytes: On `save`: the size of the file.
returns.mark: On `load`: where the log ended as the load was sent. `log` and `log_wait` take it as `since_mark`.
returns.taps: On `load`, when a count or capture watch had to be set again: `rearmed` lists each `ref`, `unarmed` the ones that could not be, each with `why`.

refuses: A name with no letter or digit, of digits only, or longer than 64 characters (`bad_argument`).
A `save` under a name that already has a file (`bad_argument`).
A `load` of a name with no state, or whose `.sav` is no regular file (`unknown_ref`).
A `load` of a state saved from another program than the one running; the message names it (`needs_call`).
A state of another DOSBox-X version, memory size or machine type, or any other refusal the emulator prints (`unexpected_answer`).
A DOSBox-X whose debugger has no `SAVESTATE` and `LOADSTATE` commands (`no_channel`).
why: Both methods are the debugger's own commands, `SAVESTATE` and `LOADSTATE`, sent over the debugger connection: no window, no menu, no dialog, and no focus taken from your screen.

They need the debugger stopped: a load while the program runs would replace the timer handlers the emulator is in the middle of calling. So a running program is stopped for the command and resumed afterwards, and `paused` says so.

A load replaces the whole machine, so a state of another version, memory size or machine type is refused. A state of another program is the one a call can mend: the emulator loads a state only while the program it was saved from runs. Run until that program runs, then load.
why_more: A state of another program is refused with the machine left as it was. That is the case at the stop before DOS boots, where no program runs yet.
`save` alters nothing. A `load` marks the session `altered` even when the emulator refuses it part of the way through, since part of the machine may have been replaced.
A name is never digits only, because the emulator's own slot files are `<n>.sav` in the same folder. The command's own answer is the confirmation: a refusal the emulator prints comes back quoted.
A load can move the program's load address. Each breakpoint saved by symbol name is then cleared at its old address and set again, because the debugger's own rows outlive a load.

`mark` is where each log ended as the load was sent, the same position for `guest`, `emulator` and `all`. `log` and `log_wait` take it as `since_mark` to read what came after. It is a position in the file, not a moment, so a line written before the load and not yet flushed lands after it.

A cancelled call releases a program it stopped. A cancelled `save` removes the file it began, and a cancelled `load` that was already sent marks the session `altered`, since part of the machine may be replaced.

symbols_load.what: Load your program's symbol table from a file your toolchain writes, so that other tools take names in place of addresses.
symbols_load.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, stopped at its play screen, where DOS has loaded it at segment 08DF.
symbols_load.ask: Load the game's symbols from `demos/bricks/bricks.sym`; DOS loaded it at segment 08DF.
symbols_load.reads: All 65 symbols of the file are in the debugger, none renamed, at linear `0x8df0`, which is segment 08DF times 16. `replaced` means this table stands alone: any earlier one is gone.

arguments.path: The symbol file, by absolute path: the output of `nm`, or a link map from GNU `ld`, Borland or Open Watcom.
arguments.base: The linear address the program is loaded at, for a file without sections: an integer or `0x` text. Left out, it is measured through `base_from`.
arguments.base_from: Where the base is measured when `base` is left out: a segment register, or a selector as four hex digits such as `00AF`. Left out, `CS`.
arguments.pattern: A regular expression: only the symbols whose full name matches are loaded. Left empty, all are.
arguments.keep_noise: `true` keeps the section labels, the names that start with a dot. Left out, they are dropped.
arguments.section_bases: For a map with sections: the linear address of each section by its index, as `{"1": "0x401000"}`. Never together with `base`.
arguments.types: A file, by absolute path, that says what type some symbols are, so a watch on one needs no format. Left empty, none is typed.

returns.loaded: How many symbols this load put into the debugger, counted from the list the debugger saves back.
returns.renamed: How many names were cut or numbered to fit the debugger's 15 characters. Lookups still take the full name.
returns.table_mode: `accumulated` when the load added to the table already there, `replaced` when it took its place because the base changed.
returns.checked: The executable the table was compared with (`against`) and how many symbols `agree`, or why it could not be checked.
returns.pending: `true` when the program was running: the table reaches the debugger at the next stop.
returns.declarations: What became of the saved breakpoints and watches under the new table: `rearmed`, `stale`, `unresolved`, `ambiguous` or `unarmable`.

refuses: Both `base` and `section_bases`, or a map with sections and no `section_bases` (`bad_argument`).
A file without sections at a real-mode stop, with neither `base` nor a selector number in `base_from` (`bad_argument`).
A program that is running, with no `base` (`not_stopped`).
A Borland or Watcom map most of whose rows cannot be read (`bad_argument`).
A table that disagrees with the executable beside it: one of the two is another build's (`bad_argument`).
Two names that differ only in case; the message names both lines (`bad_argument`).
Filters that leave no symbol, or more names than the debugger's list holds (`bad_argument`).
why: The base is measured from the stopped machine, through the descriptor of `base_from`: under DPMI, the DOS protected-mode interface, it is only decided when the program loads. In real mode a register has no descriptor, so a file without sections needs `base` there. At base 0 every symbol would load without complaint, at its raw offset.

The table is checked against the executable beside it, the file of the same name ending in `.exe`. An old table puts every name a few bytes off and nothing in it says so. Which of the two is out of date the check cannot know; once that executable is written again, every reply carries `image_changed_on_disk`.

The debugger keeps 15 characters of a name, so a longer one is cut, and names that would then be equal get a `~n`; read `renamed`, which counts both. Lookups on the server take the full names and ignore case, which is why two names that differ only in case are refused.
why_more: The debugger only adds to its list. A second load at the same base adds to the table. A load at another base replaces the server's table, and the old rows stay in the debugger, unseen by `symbols_find`, until `close` and a new `start`.

A load that fails after the debugger took the list leaves the rows there while the reply is `INVALID`, and a second try adds a copy. The list holds 65535 names at most, so a load that would pass that is refused before it begins. A program that later runs another program at another base is not measured again.

Loading writes two temporary files, `SYMS.BIN` and `SYMSBK.BIN`, in the emulator's working directory and removes them; a file already there under either name is refused. `loaded` is counted from the second, which the debugger saves back, because the debugger reports success even for a file name it cut short.

A row of a 32-bit Borland map is a section index and an offset inside that section, and its `Start` column is no help: every section starts at zero there. The server does not read the linked program, hence `section_bases`. Such a map describes a Win32 program: if every breakpoint is refused afterwards, that is why.

- `parsed` counts the symbols the file holds and `kept` the ones that passed the filters.
- `unreadable` counts the lines that could not be read, as `nm -C` writes when a name has spaces.
- `excluded_sections`, `excluded_pattern` and `excluded_unplaceable` count what the filters dropped. `unencodable` lists names the debugger cannot hold and `unencodable_total` counts them.
- `overlay_idle` counts the loaded symbols a Borland map marks `idle`. They are part of `kept`, and what the linker means by the mark is not settled.
- `truncated_names` counts the cut names and `disambiguated` the ones given a `~n`.
- `base`, `limit` and `descriptor` are what was measured; `base_from` says `caller` when you gave the base.
- `debugger_holds` is every row the debugger holds now, given when that is more than `loaded`.
- `table_total` is the size of the server's table now, `bytes` the size of the file given to the debugger, `symbols_typed` the names `types` typed.
Writing the file is your build's job, with your toolchain's `nm`. Write it to a temporary file and move it: `>` empties the file before `nm` runs, and a half-written table would be trusted.

| symbol file | where its addresses come from |
|---|---|
| `nm` output, a GNU `ld` map, a real-mode Borland map | one `base`, given or measured through `base_from` |
| a 32-bit Borland map, an Open Watcom map | `section_bases`, one address per section |

The file is read leniently: a byte that is not UTF-8, such as a code page 437 character in a DOS map, is replaced and the rest is read. `base` and `section_bases` are two arguments because one value cannot honestly be a number for one file and a table for another.

The names come from a text listing your toolchain writes. A DJGPP executable's own COFF symbols serve only to check it. The debugger's own `IV` command takes one address typed at its console, so the whole list goes in as the file the debugger loads. A function the compiler inlined, such as a `static` one at `-O3`, has no symbol.

symbols_find.what: Find a symbol's address by its name, or find which symbol an address falls in.
symbols_find.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, stopped at its play screen with its symbols loaded.
symbols_find.reads: Five symbols start with `ball`, and all five came back. The whole reply, below, lists each with its offset and its linear address.

arguments.name: The symbol to look up, case ignored. An exact match wins; with none, every symbol that starts with it is listed, by section and offset.
arguments.offset: An offset as the toolchain wrote it, before any base. The reply is the nearest symbol at or below it.
arguments.section: The section `offset` is in, by its index, for a table loaded with `section_bases`. A table without sections needs none.
arguments.linear: A linear address, never a `SEG:OFF`: an integer or `0x` text. The reply is the nearest symbol at or below it.
arguments.limit: How many symbols a name lookup lists: 1 to 50. Left out, 10; a lookup by address does not use it.

returns.symbols: By name: the first `limit` matches, each with `name`, `kind`, `offset`, `section`, `addr` and `idle`.
returns.symbols_total: By name: how many symbols matched.
returns.truncated: By name: `true` when more matched than `symbols` lists.
returns.name: By address: the nearest symbol at or below the address, with the fields of a row of `symbols`.
returns.delta: By address: how many bytes the address is past that symbol's start.
returns.addr: The symbol's linear address: its `offset` plus the base the table was loaded at.

refuses: More or fewer than one of `name`, `offset` and `linear`: one question per call (`bad_argument`).
A session with no table loaded (`no_channel`).
An `offset` with no `section` on a table with sections, or a `section` on a table without (`bad_argument`).
An address below every symbol, or a section the table does not have (`unknown_ref`).
why: The table is the server's own copy, not read from the machine, so the lookup answers while the program runs. Its names are whole, never cut to the debugger's 15 characters, and leave out what the load's filters dropped.

`delta` is a distance past the symbol's start because the table holds no sizes. `kind` is `nm`'s letter for the symbol's type, mostly `?` from a link map. `idle` is Borland's own mark on a row, always `false` for `nm` and GNU maps.

comment_list.what: List every saved comment of this program, each with its address and whether it resolves now.
comment_list.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen, right after the comment of the entry below was added.
comment_list.ask: Which comments are saved for this game?
comment_list.reads: One comment is saved, and `truncated` is `false`: the reply lists every one.

returns.comments: The comments this reply shows. Each row has `ref`, `text`, `addr` once resolved, `state`, and `why` when it does not resolve.
returns.comments_total: How many comments are saved, listed or not.
returns.truncated: `true` when there are more comments than the reply lists. `comment_write(method="save")` writes them all.
returns.declarations: The saved breakpoints file the comments live in: its `path`, and `persistent`, which is `true` for a file on disk.

why: It reads the saved comments and types nothing at the debugger, so it answers while the program runs. Rows come in the order they were saved.
why_more: What `state` says of a comment:

- `resolved`: its `ref` resolves to an address now.
- `unresolved`: no such symbol in the loaded symbol table.
- `ambiguous`: its name matches several symbols.
- `stale`: a raw `SEG:OFF` not known to be this build's.
- `unarmable`: its address cannot be worked out now, for instance a protected-mode `SEG:OFF` until a stop reads its selector's base.

- Each row also carries `by`, `cpu`, `created_at`, `origin`, `inherited` and `age_s`, as a saved breakpoint's row does.
- A row's `cpu` is always an object with `available` set to `false` and a `why`: a DOS machine has one cpu.
- `orphan: true` is on a row saved with no record of its session.
- While the program runs the reply adds `last_stop`.

comment_write.what: Change the saved comments: add or delete one, or save them all to a file and load them back.
comment_write.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped on its play screen with `bricks.sym` loaded, which names the routine `brick_hit`.
comment_write.ask: Leave a note on the routine that removes a brick: AL is the row, BL the column.

call.text: AL = row, BL = column of the brick that falls

comment_write.reads: The comment is saved on `brick_hit`, which is the linear address `0x90b8`. Nothing was there before, so `replaced_comments` is empty.

head: method
what it does
rows: Puts `text` on `ref`. A comment already there is replaced.
Writes every comment to the file `dest`.
Reads the comment file at `path` into the saved comments, all or nothing.

arguments.ref: For `add` and `delete`: a symbol or a `SEG:OFF`.
arguments.text: For `add`: one printable line, at most 237 UTF-8 bytes.
arguments.dest: For `save`: the file to write, an absolute or `~`-led path. A comment file already there is replaced; any other file is refused.
arguments.path: For `load`: the comment file to read, an absolute path.

returns.comment: `add`: the comment as saved, a row as `comment_list` gives it.
returns.replaced_comments: `add` and `load`: the comments whose text was replaced, as they were.
returns.dropped_comments: `save`: comments only the replaced file held, each by `ref`. They are gone from the file.
returns.added: `load`: how many comments are new. `unchanged` counts those already saved with the same text, `parsed` the rows read.

refuses: An argument the method does not take (`bad_argument`).
`add`, `delete` or `load` while the program runs (`not_stopped`).
A `ref` that is a pointer or adds an offset, or a `text` that is empty, too long or not one printable line (`bad_argument`).
A name the symbol table defines twice (`ambiguous_ref`).
A `delete` whose `ref` matches no comment (`unknown_ref`).
A `dest` that is the saved breakpoints file itself, a link, or a file that is not a comment file (`bad_argument`).
A `save` while two comments sit on one address: delete one first (`bad_argument`).
A saved breakpoints file that cannot be written: nothing changes (`host_failed`).
why: One address shows one comment, however it is spelled: `start`, `0824:000B` and `0814:010B` can name one byte. An `add` where a comment exists replaces its text.
`save` and `load` are how a project keeps its comments under version control beside its symbol file. `load` is all or nothing, and the file wins where both comment an address.
why_more:
- A comment sets nothing in the debugger, so it never stops the program.
- A symbol the loaded symbol table lacks is saved `unresolved`, and resolves once a table has it.
- A raw `SEG:OFF` comment is `stale` while the build it was written over is not the one loaded, as a raw breakpoint is.
- Comments a rebuild or a `load` brought to one address are all kept. A call reaches the one whose `ref` it spells.
- The file's `cpu` column is written empty, since a DOS machine has one processor. A file that fills it is refused.
- The file has no build column: a raw address is trusted for the build it is loaded into.
- A file saved before `symbols_load`, or while the program runs, can hold two rows that a later stop resolves to one byte.
- A `load` keeps both such rows and names them in `note`. A `save` refuses them until one is deleted.
- A `load` that gives a `stale` raw comment the text it already holds adopts it into this session and build.
- A row a `load` cannot resolve at this stop is kept `unarmable`, its `why` naming the stop it waits for. An `add` refuses such an address.
- `comments_total`, `dropped_total` and `replaced_total` count the whole lists; `truncated` says a list was cut. `declarations` names the saved breakpoints file, as in `comment_list`.

send_keys.what: Send keystrokes to the DOS program, and check in its log that it reacted to them.
send_keys.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, running, with the ball waiting on the paddle. The example session sends this key as one step of a `perform`.
send_keys.ask: Press the space bar to serve the ball, and tell me whether the game logged the serve.
send_keys.reads: "reaction seen" means the game wrote a line matching `SERVE$` to its log after the key. One key (`posted`) went in as two scan-code bytes, each a command (`frames`) to the helper inside DOS, the `guest` route.

arguments.keys: The names of the keys to send, in order: at most 64, such as `enter`, `a`, `f1` or `left`.
arguments.modifiers: Keys held around the others: `shift`, `ctrl` (or `control`) and `alt` (or `option`), in any case. Left out, none.
arguments.expect: A regular expression for the line the program writes to its log when it reacts. Left out, nothing is checked.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the `expect` line, up to 600. Left out, 10; refused without `expect`.
arguments.action: `press` taps each key; `down` presses and holds, `up` lets go, so a key can stay held across calls. Left out, `press`.

returns.verify: Whether the program reacted. `checked` is `false` with no `expect`; else `verdict` is `TARGET` (the line came, in `line`) or `TIMEOUT` (it did not).
returns.posted: How many keys were sent into the program. `bytes` is how many scan-code bytes they made, and `frames` how many commands the helper took.
returns.route: Which way the input went in: always `guest` here, through the helper inside DOS.
returns.polls: From a stopped machine, how many frames it ran while the keys went in. The reply then also carries the stop it was left at.
returns.frame_after: While the guest runs, the display frame right after the input went in; `frame_before` is the one before. Unavailable, with why, when `RUNSTATE` prints no frame count.
returns.delivered: Only on a send that failed: `false` when nothing went in and the call can be sent again, `true` when part of it did.

refuses: A key or a modifier it has no name for; a DOS keyboard has no command key (`bad_argument`).
No key at all, or more than 64 (`bad_argument`).
`seconds` without `expect`, an `expect` that is no valid pattern, or an `expect` with no log to read (`bad_argument`).
No helper answering inside DOS, or a helper of another protocol version (`no_channel`).
A stopped machine on a build whose debugger has no `RUNSTATE` command (`no_channel`).
A breakpoint that stops the machine while the keys go in, or during the `expect` wait (`wait_stopped`).
An emulator busy inside a long host call, which answers nothing: no key was sent (`host_failed`).
why: An input sent to a running program lands whenever it arrives, an instant no replay can find again. Sent to a machine stopped at the debugger, it goes in as the machine runs frame by frame. The reply counts those frames in `polls` and carries the stop, so an exported session can replay the input.

The commands go in a BIOS timer tick apart, so a game that reads its keyboard once a frame sees a key go down before it comes up. That is also why a call takes at most 64 keys: every scan-code byte is one command, and the session answers nothing else until the last one is in.

`expect` is matched against what the program literally writes, so read its log once first: a program that logs `key down x mods=4` for alt+x is telling you its pattern. A miss is `TIMEOUT` beside what was sent, because a swallowed key and a key never sent are different facts.
why_more: **The helper**

The server takes the emulated COM1 for the helper and switches on DOSBox-X's integration device itself: your conf needs neither, and one that sets `serial1` loses it. `start` loads the helper on the first drive letter from Y: down that the conf's `[autoexec]` does not mount; a conf that mounts them all is refused.

The helper announces itself in the program's log. The first input is refused `no_channel` when that line is missing or names another protocol version; with no `logfile` there is no line to read, and input goes out unchecked.

- It works from the serial port's interrupt, so a game that takes over the timer still gets its input. One that also masks IRQ 4 does not.
- It runs on the stack of the program it interrupts, so a small private stack has to leave room for it.
- Each command is acknowledged before the next goes: a lost byte is sent again, and no command runs twice.
- The tick between commands is the program's own emulated time, which a slow host stretches; without the `RUNSTATE` debugger command it is real time.

If a breakpoint stops the machine inside the helper, `resume` from that stop: moving the instruction pointer out leaves the helper ignoring every later input. A `breakpoint_interrupt` on INT 33h can stop there, since the helper calls INT 33h itself.
**A stopped machine**

A code breakpoint that stops one of the frames ends the send there (`wait_stopped`), with the commands already taken in. A stop from a change watch or an interrupt breakpoint looks like the end of a frame and counts as one, as in `run_for`.

`expect` is then waited for one frame per look, and its `seconds` are the program's own time, so a replay that misses runs the same frames. In the stop the reply carries, `e9` is what the program logged during every frame run, and `watches` are as the last frame read them.
**No reaction seen**

A machine that stops during the `expect` wait is refused `wait_stopped`, with `last_stop`. A command sent before the stop lands at the next `resume`, and later ones are not sent. So a key whose press stopped the machine stays down until a later send lets it go.

- Whether an input went in before such a stop is for the program's log to say: read `log` since the send.
- An emulator that died is `verify.checked: false`, never a swallowed key.
- A program that writes nothing to its log gives `expect` nothing to match.
- `seen_before_waiting: true`: the line came while the keys were still going in. It is still this input's reaction.
- In a `perform` or a `drive`, a `TIMEOUT` ends the list there.
- A new session's first key can be swallowed while DOS settles: send it once more before looking for a dialog.

`verify` in full: `checked`, `expected` (the pattern), `seen`, `verdict`, `waited_s`; when seen, `line`, `seen_before_waiting`, `lines_before` and `lines_total`; on a `TIMEOUT`, `note`, `arrived_during` and `lines_examined`. `arrived_during` counts the lines the program wrote during the wait: zero means it wrote nothing at all. `why` says why nothing was checked, and a stop during the wait adds `stopped_during_wait` and `lines_on_disk`.
**Keys**

A key sent while a dialog is closing can be swallowed. To send it once the screen has settled: `stop`, `run_for` a few frames, read `screen_signature`, and repeat until two reads agree; then send the key. A stopped machine's time moves only when `run_for` moves it, so the wait costs the program no time.

- The keys go in as set 1 scan codes, composed by the server.
- A cancelled call lets go of every key it had pressed, so none stays down repeating in the program.
**A send the emulator could not take**

While the emulator is inside a long host call, such as the first long-name open in a folder of very many files, its debugger does not answer. A send that meets this before writing anything is refused `host_failed` with `delivered: false`. Nothing went in: send it again once `status` answers.

A send cut part-way answers `delivered: true` with how many commands went in and how many did not: send only what was not written. A key it pressed and could not let go stays down until the session's next input, which lets it go first and says so in `note`.
Keys a call holds on purpose (`action="down"`) are not let go this way, and loading a saved state forgets any key still owed.

send_mouse.what: Move the DOS program's mouse pointer, press its buttons or drag, and read back where the pointer ended.
send_mouse.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, running with the mouse in control of the paddle, after `screen_map_find` recognised the play screen. `court` is an area of the demo's screen map.
send_mouse.ask: Put the mouse pointer on the middle of the court and show me where it ended.
send_mouse.reads: The pointer went to the centre of `court`: pixel 240,100 of a 320x200 screen, 480,100 in the mouse driver's own coordinates. `driver_arrived` speaks for the driver's pointer only; `motion` says the move also went in as mouse motion.

arguments.x: Where the pointer goes, across, in `units`. Give it with `y`; left out, the pointer stays where it is.
arguments.y: Where the pointer goes, down, in `units`. Give it with `x`.
arguments.button: The button that acts: `left`, `right` or `middle`. Left out, the left one when an `action` is named, else none.
arguments.action: What the button does: `click`, `double`, `triple`, `down`, `up` or `drag`. Left out, a click when a `button` is named, else no button.
arguments.units: `screen`, the default, counts character cells in a text mode and pixels in a graphics one, as `screen_view` does. `mouse` is the mouse driver's own coordinates.
arguments.expect: A regular expression for the line the program logs when it reacts, as in [`send_keys`](#send_keys). Left out, nothing is checked.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the `expect` line, up to 600. Left out, 10; refused without `expect`.
arguments.target: A control, a named area of the screen the latest `screen_map_find` recognised, in place of `x` and `y`. The pointer goes to its centre.
arguments.to_x: Where a drag ends, across, in `units`. Only with `action="drag"`, and with `to_y`.
arguments.to_y: Where a drag ends, down, in `units`. Only with `action="drag"`, and with `to_x`.

returns.pointer: Where the pointer ended: `screen` in screen units, `mouse` in the driver's coordinates with its range, the `buttons` held and the `bios_mode`.
returns.arrived: Whether the pointer is on the point asked for. It comes only when something could check that: the program's own pointer, or `units="mouse"`.
returns.driver_arrived: In place of `arrived` for a plain screen move: whether the driver's pointer got there, which a program with its own pointer may not follow. `asked` holds what was sent.
returns.motion: `true` when the move also went in as mouse motion, which a program that reads motion needs. Otherwise it says why not.
returns.verify: Whether the program reacted, as in [`send_keys`](#send_keys).
returns.frame_after: While the guest runs, the display frame right after the input went in; `frame_before` is the one before. Unavailable, with why, when `RUNSTATE` prints no frame count.

refuses: No move and no button, or `x` without `y` (`bad_argument`).
A point off the screen, or a screen mode of unknown size, where `units="mouse"` still works (`bad_argument`).
`target` together with `x`, `y` or `units="mouse"` (`bad_argument`).
A drag without both ends, or `to_x` and `to_y` without a drag (`bad_argument`).
A `target` with no screen recognised by `screen_map_find`, or after the screen mode changed (`needs_call`).
A `target` the recognised screen does not have (`unknown_ref`).
No helper inside DOS, or a stopped machine on a build without the `RUNSTATE` debugger command (`no_channel`).
A breakpoint that stops the machine during the send or the `expect` wait (`wait_stopped`).
An emulator busy inside a long host call: nothing was sent (`host_failed`).
why: DOS programs read the mouse in different ways: some ask the driver where the pointer is, many read how far it moved, and some drive a PS/2 mouse themselves. So a move goes in twice: first as motion, which reaches all of them, then as an exact position. `motion` says whether the first half went in.

The pointer that moves is the mouse driver's, the one DOSBox-X provides: a mouse driver loaded inside DOS reads its own hardware and is not reached. A program that keeps a pointer of its own, adding up motion, can end somewhere else, so a plain screen move answers only `driver_arrived`.

A [screen map](read.md#screen_map_write) is a file that names a program's screens and the areas of each. When it also says where the program keeps its pointer, the server reads that pointer and corrects the move, and `arrived` then speaks for it.
why_more: **How programs read the mouse**

DOSBox-X passes on your own mouse's motion only while its window has captured the mouse, which no session does. So the helper sends the motion itself, through DOSBox-X's integration device, then sets the position.

- Motion counters (INT 33h AX=0Bh) and movement events (a handler set with AX=0Ch): reached by the motion.
