- A PS/2 mouse the program drives through the BIOS: reached too, as DOSBox-X scales the motion, so a move of a few units can reach it as none.
- The driver's position: set exactly (AX=04h) after the motion.
- A build whose integration device takes no motion only sets the position, and `motion` says why.
**`pointer` in full**

- `screen`: `x`, `y`, `width`, `height` in screen units; unavailable in a mode of unknown size.
- `mouse`: `x`, `y` in the driver's coordinates, with its range `max_x`, `max_y`.
- `buttons` held, `bios_mode`, and `vbe_mode` under a VBE mode.
- `program`: the program's own pointer when a screen map gives it: `x`, `y`, and `corrections`, how many times the move was corrected.
- `program.reach`: when it did not get there, the span (`x`, `y`, low and high) it covered between the driver's two corners.
- `program.range_widened`: the driver range (`x`, `y`) the server set, in the reply that widened it.

Under a VBE mode the BIOS mode byte is the emulated card's own number, so the helper asks VBE for the mode and its resolution (INT 10h 4F03h and 4F01h). The units are then that resolution: pixels, or character cells for a VBE text mode.

Each screen unit covers several driver coordinates, and the move aims at the middle of them. The driver rounds to its own steps and a program divides its range back, as Deluxe Paint does with eight coordinates a pixel. Aimed at a unit's first coordinate, the pointer could land in the unit before.

`arrived` is checked in the units asked: any driver coordinate inside the unit counts. It is `false` when the driver's rounding or the program's own range left the pointer in another unit, and `asked` then gives the driver coordinates sent. A text mode snaps the pointer to its character cell, and the reply reports where it ended.
**A program with a pointer of its own**

Its pointer is read only on a stopped machine, in `units="screen"`, in a mode of known size; otherwise `pointer.program` says why it was not read. A drag's end is not corrected. When the target is past what the driver's range lets that pointer reach, the server widens the range once; `range_widened` then shows in every reply's `session`.

Allegro's default DOS mouse driver keeps its own pointer this way. With `mouse = I33` under `[mouse]` in the program's `allegro.cfg` it reads the driver instead, sets the range to its screen, and is pointed at by pixel like any other program.
**Buttons**

- `double` and `triple` are two and three clicks a timer tick apart, close enough for a program that counts them.
- A button with no `x`, `y` acts where the pointer is. A move and a button in one call move first.
- A cancelled call does not let go of a button it pressed, since `action="down"` holds one on purpose.
- A call with a button and no move answers `arrived: true`.

A click that fires a code breakpoint ends the call `wait_stopped`, stopped machine or running: the program reacts within a frame, before the pointer is read back. In a `perform` that step is `step_failed`. A read-back that fails after the commands went in is refused with `delivered: true`, so nothing is sent twice.
**The rest of the reply**
With `target`, the reply adds `target`, `screen` (the screen recognised) and `identified_at_stop`, the number of the stop at which `screen_map_find` recognised it.

In a [`perform`](sequences.md#perform) run with `summaries`, each frame a send ran on a stopped machine is a numbered stop, and only the last one is in a reply. `stops.unaccounted` counts the stops numbered during the list that no step's reply shows, so a few sends make it large.
The helper, a stopped machine, `expect` and a failed send work as under [`send_keys`](#send_keys). With no `logfile` the mouse goes in unchecked too.
**The pointer you see**

With a window and its border, the first move also shows an orange pointer: the DOS mouse driver's default graphics pointer, one cell per screen pixel. In a graphics mode it is the size of the program's own pointer, whatever the window's size. The mouse driver's pointer is at its new place at once; the orange one glides there briefly. It is never in a capture, and a failure to draw it fails nothing.

captures.what: List the files this session's tools wrote, each read again now: whether it is still there, its size, what it holds.

returns.captures: One row per file: `kind`, `path`, `present` and `bytes`. A recording adds `complete` and what it holds, by kind.

why: Every file is read again when it has changed, so the list says what is on disk now, and it answers while the program runs. A file deleted since stays listed, with `present: false` and no `bytes`.

First come the files the session's tools wrote, in the order written. Then come the videos of a session started with `capture_video`, largest last; two is normal, since the recording restarts when the program changes video mode.
An AVI's `complete: false` is not damage: frames come out of such a file. For a WAV, a DRO or a MIDI file it is a header that disagrees with the file: one its writer has not closed, or a damaged one.
why_more:
| `kind` | what the row adds |
|---|---|
| `avi` | `complete`, `riff_avi` (it opens as an AVI), `avi_frames` |
| `wav` | `complete`, `samples`, `channels`, `sample_rate_hz` |
| `dro` | `complete`, `opl_pairs`, `opl_ms` |
| `mid` | `complete`, `midi_bytes` |
Any other row's `kind` is its file's extension, or `series` for a series.
`start`'s `program` runs after the configuration's `[autoexec]` section, so an autoexec that ends in `exit` quits the emulator first. A list with no `avi` row is the sign.
captures.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, at the end of a session that saved pictures, a video, a sound file and a dump of memory.
captures.ask: List the files this session has written so far.
captures.reads: The session wrote ten files. `captures` has a row for each, with its kind, its path and whether it is still there.

capture_frame.what: Extract one frame of a video the session recorded to a PNG file.

arguments.frame: The frame to extract, counted from 0 at the video's first frame.
arguments.dest: A new path for the PNG, absolute or starting with `~`. The file is a PNG whatever its extension.
arguments.capture_path: The video to take the frame from, such as one `record` wrote. Left empty, the largest video of a session started with `capture_video`.

returns.sha256: The file's SHA-256: the value a line of reference checksums holds for `image_compare(method="golden")`.
returns.capture_path: The video the frame came from.

refuses: A `%` anywhere in `dest`, or a `dest` that exists (`bad_argument`).
No `capture_path`, in a session not started with `capture_video` (`no_channel`).
No `capture_path`, in a session whose video is not written yet (`unexpected_answer`).
A frame past the end of the video, or a computer with no `ffmpeg` on its `PATH` (`host_failed`).
why: The still is always a PNG, whatever `dest` is called. Choosing the format from the extension would let `ffmpeg` answer a frame past the end with an empty video file and no error.

A `%` anywhere in `dest` is refused before anything runs: `ffmpeg` reads the whole path as a numbering pattern, and the still is one file. Name that file, or take several frames with `series_capture`.
The frame shows what was displayed, in any video mode, because it comes out of a video. The call reads a file, so it answers while the program runs.
capture_frame.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, after the [`record`](#record) example filmed 110 frames in which a brick falls.
capture_frame.ask: Take frame 104 out of the video second-brick.avi and save it as brick-gone.png.
capture_frame.reads: Frame 104 of the video, counted from 0, is now a PNG at `path`.

series_capture.what: Save chosen frames of the screen as PNGs beside a manifest, for `image_compare` to read.

arguments.at_frames: The frames to keep, as an ascending list of frame numbers. Give this or `first` and `last`, never both.
arguments.first: The first frame of an evenly spaced range, given with `last`.
arguments.last: The last frame of the range. A series holds at most 1000 frames.
arguments.step: The spacing of the range: every `step`-th frame from `first`. Left out, 1.
arguments.crop: The rectangle of the screen each PNG holds, `[x, y, width, height]`. Left out, the whole screen.
arguments.dest: A new folder for the series, absolute or starting with `~`, which outlives `close`. Left empty, a folder in the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.
arguments.capture_path: The video to take the frames from, such as one `record` wrote. Left empty, the largest video of a session started with `capture_video`.

returns.manifest: The path of the series' manifest, `manifest.json`; the PNGs sit beside it, named by frame as `f000123.png`.
returns.count: How many frames were written; `first` and `last` are their lowest and highest numbers.
returns.distinct: How many different pictures the series holds. One means nothing changed on screen.
returns.kept_after_close: `true` when the series is in a `dest` you named, `false` when `close` deletes it.
returns.capture_path: The video the frames came from.

refuses: Both `at_frames` and a range, or neither; a list that is not ascending; more than 1000 frames (`bad_argument`).
A frame past the end of the video (`bad_argument`).
A `crop` that leaves the frame, or a `dest` that exists or holds a `%` (`bad_argument`).
No `capture_path`, in a session not started with `capture_video` (`no_channel`).
No `capture_path`, in a session whose video is not written yet (`unexpected_answer`).
A computer with no `ffmpeg` on its `PATH` (`host_failed`).
why: The frames come out of a video, so their numbers are the video's own, from 0 at its first frame. They are not the frames a stop's `frame` field counts since power-on.

The call reads a file and does not run the machine, so it answers while the program runs. A session started with `capture_video` can hold several videos: `captures` lists them, and `capture_path` picks one.
A `%` in `dest` is refused because `ffmpeg` would read the path as a numbering pattern and write somewhere else.
why_more: A video's frames are the size the emulator draws them: a 320x200 mode comes out 640x400, and a `crop` counts those pixels.
`frames_asked` is how many frames the call named, and `frame_source` says what the numbers count: `avi`, the video's own frames.
series_capture.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, after the [`record`](#record) example filmed 110 frames in which a brick falls.
series_capture.ask: Save frames 95 to 108 of the video second-brick.avi as a series in a folder named series.
series_capture.reads: Fourteen frames of the video were written, all different pictures (`distinct`). `frame_source` `avi` says the numbers are the video's own, and `crop` that each PNG is the whole 640x400 frame.

snapshot.what: Save a still of the screen as it is now to a PNG file.

arguments.dest: A new path for the PNG, absolute or starting with `~`. Left empty, the emulator's capture folder.
arguments.seconds: While the program runs: how long to wait for the picture, in seconds. Left out, 10; not used at a stop.

returns.sha256: The file's SHA-256: the value a line of reference checksums holds for `image_compare(method="golden")`.
returns.route: How the still was taken: `guest` while the program ran, `video_memory` at a stop.

refuses: While the program runs: a session with no `logfile`, or with no input helper announced in its log (`no_channel`).
While the program runs: no new PNG within `seconds` (`wait_expired`).
At a stop: a screen in a text mode, which has no picture (`no_channel`).
A `dest` that exists or is relative (`bad_argument`).
why: The still is taken one of two ways, chosen by whether the program runs. While it runs, the input helper inside DOS takes the screenshot, with no window or menu involved.

At a stop no frame is being drawn, so the still is decoded from video memory as `screen_view` decodes it: unscaled, and without running the machine. A text mode has no picture there; `screen_view` reads its text.
The running way needs a session started with `logfile`. Only the log says which input helper is loaded, and an older one would read the command as the Delete key.
snapshot.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, while the game runs with the mouse holding the paddle.
snapshot.ask: Save a picture of the screen as it is now to held.png, without stopping the game.
snapshot.reads: The `route` named `guest` is the way used while the program runs: the picture is taken inside the emulated machine. The file is at `path`.

record.what: Record an exact number of frames of the screen to an AVI video, then stop the program again.

arguments.frames: How many frames of the emulated display to record: 2 or more.
arguments.dest: An absolute `.avi` path that does not exist yet. Left empty, the file goes to the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the whole call, in seconds of your clock. Left out, 60.

returns.path: The AVI, once the reply has read it back as a finished file.
returns.avi_frames: How many frames the file's own header says it holds.
returns.ended: `true` once the capture is turned off. `false` when it could not be: there is no `path`, and it records until `close`.
returns.verdict: How the run ended, as `run_for` reports it: `ELAPSED` when every frame ran, `TIMEOUT` when `seconds` ran out first.

refuses: `frames` under 2, or a `dest` that is not a new `.avi` path (`bad_argument`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A video capture already on, as in a session started with `capture_video` (`no_channel`).
A build whose debugger has no `CAPTURE` command (`no_channel`).
A file that does not read back as a finished AVI with a frame in it (`readback_refused`).
why: The recording is counted in frames of the emulated display, one per vertical retrace, so no time of your clock goes into the file. The debugger's `CAPTURE` command turns the video on at this stop and off at the stop the run reaches.
No window or menu is involved, so a session with no window records as one with a window does. A video already on is refused, never ended by a second switch.
One frame is written per frame run, but a run can write none for its first. The run from the stop `start` leaves is one: the display has drawn nothing yet.
why_more: The capture is turned off whatever the run did, a cancelled call included. One that could not be turned off answers `ended: false`.
The reply is also a stop: it carries `verdict` and the fields `run_for` returns, with the readings taken at each stop.
record.on: On Bricks, the game this repository builds, stopped in play at frame 36, shortly before the ball knocks down its second brick.
record.ask: Record the next 110 frames of the screen to a video named second-brick.avi.
record.reads: `ELAPSED` means the 110 frames ran, from frame 36 to 146, and the capture was turned off (`ended`). The file holds 109 frames: the first frame of this run wrote none.

audio_record.what: Record an exact number of frames of sound to a WAV, a DRO or a MIDI file, then stop the program again.

head: kind
what is recorded
rows: The mixer's output: everything the machine plays, as samples.
The writes to the OPL chip's registers, as a DRO 2.0 file.
The MIDI bytes the program sends, as a MIDI file.

arguments.frames: How many frames of the emulated display the recording lasts: 1 or more.
arguments.dest: A path that does not exist yet, absolute or starting with `~`. Left empty, the file stays where the emulator wrote it.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the whole call, in seconds of your clock. Left out, 60.

returns.path: The file, once it has been checked. Unavailable, with the reason, when the run had no OPL note or MIDI byte.
returns.emulated_s: For a WAV: the emulated time the recording spans, in seconds.
returns.sample_min: For a WAV: the lowest sample value, beside `sample_max`. The two equal mean a constant level: silence.
returns.opl_pairs: For a DRO: how many register writes and delays the file holds; `opl_ms` is its length in milliseconds.
returns.files: For a DRO, when the OPL writer began a new file during the run: every file, each with its `path` and `bytes`.
returns.ended: `true` once the capture is turned off. `false` when it could not be: there is no `path`, and it records until `close`.

refuses: `frames` under 1, or a `dest` that exists (`bad_argument`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
That kind of capture already on, or a build whose debugger has no `CAPTURE` command (`no_channel`).
A WAV that holds no sample, or whose samples miss the run's emulated time by more than 2 mixer ticks (`readback_refused`).
A DRO or a MIDI file whose header disagrees with the file (`readback_refused`).
why: The recording is counted in frames of the emulated display, as [`record`](#record) counts them: `CAPTURE` turns the kind on at this stop and off at the stop the run reaches. The file holds what was emulated in between.

Each file is checked before its path is given. A WAV's header must agree with its file, whose two sizes the emulator fills only at close, and its samples with the run's emulated time. The mixer works in ticks of an emulated millisecond, so one tick at each end is allowed.
Silence is reported, never refused: it is a fact about the program. The OPL writer opens its file at the first note and the MIDI writer at the first byte, so a run with neither has no file.
why_more: A `readback_refused` that comes and goes is the configuration's clock first. When your computer cannot run the program's fixed cycles in real time, the mixer loses whole blocks and the WAV falls short. Lower the fixed `cycles` and record again.

- A DRO must be a DRO 2.0 file whose header's length is the file's: the register state at its first event, then each write.
- A MIDI file must be a header and a track whose length reaches the end of the file; `midi_bytes` counts its events' bytes.
- The OPL writer begins a new file after half a minute of emulated silence. `path` is then the last file, and the checks and counts are that file's alone.
audio_record.on: On Minesweeper, a game this repository builds, stopped a few frames after a click on a mine, with the explosion already sounding.
audio_record.ask: Record the sound of the next 45 frames to a file named boom.wav.
audio_record.reads: A stereo WAV of 30768 samples, about 0.64 emulated seconds. `sample_min` and `sample_max` are far apart, so the recording is not silent.

image_compare.what: Compare two pictures, two series of frames, or one region across a series, and get the difference as numbers.

head: method
what it compares
rows: Two PNGs, pixel by pixel: how many pixels differ, and where.
Two series, frame by frame: how many frames are equal, and the first that differs.
One rectangle across a series: the frames at which it changes.
A series or a folder of PNGs against a file of reference checksums.

arguments.a: The first PNG for `image`, or the first manifest for `series`. An absolute path, or one starting with `~`.
arguments.b: The second PNG or manifest, compared with `a`.
arguments.crop: The rectangle to compare, `[x, y, width, height]`, for every method but `golden`. Left out, the whole picture.
arguments.shift: For `image`: `[dx, dy]`, how far `b` is moved before the two are compared. Left out, no move.
arguments.tolerance: For `image`: the difference in one colour component still counted as equal, 0 to 255. Left out, 0.
arguments.manifest: For `region` and `golden`: the series to read, by the path of its manifest.
arguments.measure: For `region`, what is followed: the rectangle's `signature`, its `changed_pixels` since the frame before, or its `match` with `ref`. Left out, `signature`.
arguments.ref: For the measure `match`: the PNG, of the crop's size, the rectangle is compared with.
arguments.threshold: For `match`: the fraction of the rectangle's pixels that must equal `ref`, above 0 and at most 1. Left out, 0.98.
arguments.limit: For `region` and `golden`: how many items each list shows, 1 to 1000. Left out, 40; the whole count is beside the list.
arguments.dir: For `golden`: a folder of PNGs to check, in place of `manifest`.
arguments.checksums: For `golden`: the file of reference checksums, in the format `shasum -a 256` writes.

returns.differing_pixels: For `image`: how many pixels differ by more than `tolerance`. Zero means the two are equal over the rectangle compared.
returns.bbox: For `image`: the rectangle that holds every differing pixel, `[x, y, width, height]` in the coordinates of `a`.
returns.first_differing: For `series`: the first frame that differs, with its `frame` number, its `differing_pixels` and its `bbox`.
returns.differing: For `series`: how many paired frames differ. For `golden`: the names of the files whose checksum differs.
returns.transitions: For `region`: each change as `[frame, value]`, the first `limit` of them; `transitions_total` counts them all.
returns.path: For `region`: a JSON file written beside the manifest, with every transition and each frame's value.

refuses: An argument the method does not take (`bad_argument`).
Two pictures of different sizes with no `crop` that lies inside both (`bad_argument`).
A `crop` that leaves the picture, or a `shift` that moves it wholly off itself (`bad_argument`).
A path that is relative or missing, or a file that is no PNG or no `scry-series/1` manifest (`bad_argument`).
A manifest with a frame changed since it was written, or a row edited by hand (`bad_argument`).
A series that never changes, two series with no frame number in common, a region that never changes, or checksums that name no file examined (`control_silent`).
why: `image` compares the colours two pictures show, so an indexed PNG and an RGB one of the same screen are equal. `golden` compares file bytes through their checksums, so those two files differ.
Two pictures of different sizes are refused unless a `crop` lies inside both. A tool that shows a picture enlarges it by its `scale`, so take both at `scale=1` before comparing them.
A `crop` that leaves the picture is refused, never padded: a padded crop would compare pixels nobody drew.
why_more:
- `series` pairs frames by number. Frames only one series has come back in `only_in_a` and `only_in_b` as `[first, last]` ranges.
- `region` answers `start`, the first frame and its value, then the transitions. `gaps` counts the frames between one transition and the next.
- `golden` pairs files and checksum lines by file name. `matched` counts the equal ones, `missing` lists lines with no file, `extra` files with no line.
- The reply repeats the arguments it took, each path in full. For `image`, `a` and `b` come back with the file's `path` and `sha256`.
image_compare.on: On the series the Bricks example of [`series_capture`](captures.md#series_capture) wrote: 14 frames of a video in which a brick falls. The rectangle is that brick's.
image_compare.ask: In the series, at which frames does the second brick's rectangle change, and by how many pixels?
image_compare.reads: The rectangle changes at four of the 14 frames, and at frame 104, 944 of its pixels change at once: the brick is gone. Each of the `gaps` is 1, so the changes are on consecutive frames.

audio_compare.what: Measure a WAV recording, or compare two, and get loudness, silence, timing and closeness as numbers.

head: method
what it answers
rows: One recording: how loud it is, whether it is silent, when the sound begins and whether it clips.
Two recordings: whether they are equal and, if not, how close they are.

arguments.path: For `measure`: the WAV to measure, 8- or 16-bit PCM. An absolute path, or one starting with `~`.
arguments.b: For `diff`: the reference recording, of the same sample rate, `channels` and bit depth as `a`.
arguments.window: The part of the recording to read, `[from_s, to_s]` in seconds. Left out, the whole file.
arguments.channel: For `measure`: which of the file's `channels` to measure, numbered from 0. Left out, each of them.
arguments.align: For `diff`: `true` lines up where the two sounds begin before comparing them; `false` compares from the first sample. Left out, `true`.

returns.measures: For `measure`: one row for each of the `channels`, with `channel`, `peak_dbfs`, `rms_dbfs`, `silent`, `silence_spans` (its `count` and `first`), `onset_s`, `clipping_run` and `clipped`.
returns.pcm_sha256: For `measure`: the SHA-256 of the samples in the window, equal for two files that hold the same sound.
returns.exact: For `diff`: `true` when the two windows hold the same bytes.
returns.class: For `diff`, the verdict in one word: `exact`, `inaudible`, `audible` or `different`.
returns.snr_db: For `diff`: the signal-to-noise ratio of `a` against `b`, the worst of the `channels`. Unavailable when the two are equal once lined up.
returns.aligned_by_samples: For `diff`: how many samples `a` was moved to line up with `b`.

refuses: An argument the method does not take (`bad_argument`).
A file that is not 8- or 16-bit PCM, holds no sample or cannot be read (`bad_argument`).
A `window` outside the recording, or a `channel` number the file does not have (`bad_argument`).
For `diff`, two recordings that differ in sample rate, `channels` or bit depth (`bad_argument`).
For `diff`, two recordings that are both silent over the window (`control_silent`).
why: The sound itself never comes back, only numbers, so a client that cannot listen checks a recording through them.
Each of the `channels` is measured and compared on its own, never mixed down first. Mixed, one in antiphase would cancel, and two swapped ones would average to the same sound.

`diff` lines up the two sounds unless `align` is `false`, so a recording that starts a few samples later is not called different. With `align` `false`, two recordings made from the same stop are compared sample for sample.
why_more:
- A steady level that is not zero is no sound: loudness, silence and the comparison read the window less its mean.
- Two recordings whose lengths are more than a tenth of a second apart are `different`.
- The reply repeats `path`, `a`, `b` and the `window` it read.
audio_compare.on: On Minesweeper, a game this repository builds, after the [`audio_record`](captures.md#audio_record) example recorded its explosion. `b` is the reference recording the demo keeps.
audio_compare.ask: Is the explosion I recorded the same as the reference boom.wav, sample for sample?
audio_compare.reads: `exact` is `true`: the two files hold the same samples, compared from their first sample. With nothing differing there is no ratio to give, so `snr_db` is unavailable.

guest_file.what: Check a file the DOS program was meant to write on a mounted drive: whether this run wrote it, its size and its hash.

arguments.path: The file on your disk, one of the paths given to `start(guest_files=)`. An absolute path, or one starting with `~`.

returns.state: `written` when this run wrote the file. `absent`, `empty`, `unchanged` and `unreadable` come as a refusal.
returns.sha256: The SHA-256 of the file now.
returns.before: What was there before the emulator booted: `exists` and, when it did, its `bytes` and `sha256`.
returns.same_bytes: `true` when the run wrote the file again with the bytes it already held.

refuses: A path that `start(guest_files=)` did not name (`bad_argument`).
A file that is `absent`, `empty`, `unchanged` since before the run, or `unreadable` (`readback_refused`).
why: A DOS program hands a result back as a file on a mounted drive. `start(guest_files=)` records each file's size, modification time and SHA-256 before the emulator boots, and this tool compares the file with that record.
A file left by an earlier run passes any test for existence, which is why `unchanged` is refused. A file written again with the same bytes has a new time, so it is `written`, with `same_bytes`.
A file the program still holds open may not have its bytes yet: the emulator buffers them until DOS closes the file.
why_more: `close` checks each file again after the emulator has exited. On a clean quit every file the program left open has been closed and written out; an emulator that was killed may have left bytes unwritten.
A file your computer cannot read, such as a name the program made a directory of, is `unreadable`, and `close` still closes.
guest_file.on: It needs a DOS program that writes a file on a mounted drive, which neither Bricks nor Minesweeper does. The reply shown comes from a test program that is not distributed.
guest_file.ask: Did the program write OUT.TXT during this run?
guest_file.reads: `written` means this run wrote the file. Nothing was there before the emulator booted (`exists` is `false`), and the file now holds 4 bytes.

perform.what: Run a list of this server's tools in one call, in order, stopping at the first step that fails.
perform.ask: Give the paddle back to the keyboard with M, then serve with the space bar, checking the game logged each key.
perform.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, while it runs with the mouse moving the paddle.
perform.reads: Both steps ran and none failed. `still_running` says the list ended with the game running and waited for no stop; `held` is 0 because no step carried `recorded` values.

arguments.steps: The list to run: each step is `{"op": <tool>, ...}` with that tool's own arguments. Give this or `path`, never both.
arguments.path: A saved step list to replay in place of `steps`: a file under `.scry/perform/` or one `perform_export` wrote. Absolute, or starting with `~`.
arguments.settle_seconds: How long each wait for a stop may take, before a step that needs one: 0 to 600 seconds. 0 never waits; left out, 30.
arguments.summaries: `true` cuts each step's reply but the last to a short row and writes the full replies to a file. Left out, every reply comes back whole.
arguments.until_frame: A frame number, counted since power-on: the list repeats until a stop reads that frame. Needs `summaries` and a `run_for` step; left at 0, the list runs once.

returns.ran: One row per step that ran: its `op` and its full `reply`. With `summaries` a row adds its `step`, and `ran_path` and `replies_path` hold them all.
returns.held: How many steps carried `recorded`, the values a replayed step must give again, and gave them. 0 when no step carried any.
returns.failed_at: The step that failed, counted from 0, with its `op` and `reply` in `failed`. When none failed it is `available: false` with a `why`.
returns.errors: Every step refused before anything ran, each with its `step`, `op`, `code` and `message`.
returns.verdict: Comes once the list waited for a stop: `TARGET` with the stop in `stopped`, or `TIMEOUT` with a `note`. A list that waited for none says `still_running`.
returns.stops: With `summaries`, the server's own count of the stops: `stop_seq_first`, `stop_seq_last`, `surveyed` (how many a reply described), `by_cause` and `unaccounted`.

refuses: A step that names no tool, an argument its tool does not take or a value it refuses. Nothing runs, and `operations` lists the tools a step may name (`bad_argument`).
Both `steps` and `path`, neither, or an empty list (`bad_argument`).
A step that answers INVALID: the list ends there (`step_failed`).
A step whose reply differs from its `recorded` values; the reply names the `field`, the `recorded` value and what it `got` (`diverged`).
A step that needs the program stopped while it still runs and `settle_seconds` is 0 (`not_stopped`).
`until_frame` without `summaries`, without a `run_for` step, or at a frame the program has already reached (`bad_argument`).
`until_frame` on a build whose `RUNSTATE` prints no `frames=`, so there is no frame to count (`no_channel`).
A stop that reads no frame under `until_frame`, since nothing then says whether the frame came (`unexpected_answer`).
The emulator gone before a step could run (`session_broken`).
why: The whole list is checked before its first step runs, so a refusal never arrives after earlier steps changed the machine. What only a running step can know refuses at that step: a symbol against the table loaded by then, a file an earlier step writes, the cpu's mode.

A step that needs the program stopped waits up to `settle_seconds` for the stop. A wait that runs out ends the list `TIMEOUT`: the steps after it were built on what it waited for. So does a step whose own wait missed: a `log_wait` or `screen_wait` that timed out, a `send_keys` or `send_mouse` whose `expect` never came.

A step may carry `recorded`, a `{field: value}` object of its own reply, and a reply with other values ends the list. That turns a list into a test, and `perform_export` writes such lists from a session.
why_more: `until_frame` counts what happens before a frame when nobody can know how many steps that takes. Every stop a watch makes takes a step without moving the frame, so a list sized by guessing ends short, with a smaller count that looks right.

The call ends right after the first step whose stop reads the frame, even mid-list, and `frame_reached` says which. It needs a `run_for` step because `run_for` carries on past a watch's stop, where `run_to` and `step` end at the first.

On a running program the first stop starts the count. Running out of steps or seconds is a `TIMEOUT` that names the last frame read. An exported script keeps the steps the repetitions ran, never the `until_frame`.

With `summaries`, `steps_total` counts the rows and `truncated` says the reply shows fewer. Read `stops` for a count and `ran_path` for the whole table: a count made by hand from cut rows comes out wrong and looks right.

After a `resume` step the server asks the debugger's `RUNSTATE` whether the program stopped again, so a stop is never guessed from a step's name. A `step` that comes back with the program running counts as a `resume`, and a `stop` step ends the run.
A `screen_view` step returns its text in the reply and writes its picture to its `path`, answering `not_inlined: nested`.
**Steps on a running program**

- A step from the list a `not_stopped` refusal names in `answers_while_running` runs on a running program. Any other waits for a stop, `symbols_load` included even with a `base`.
- That list also names tools that are no step: `close`, `drive`, `perform`, `perform_export`, `window` and `promote`.
- A list that ends with the program running after such a step, with nothing declared that could stop it, returns at once and its `note` says why.
- `operations`, the tools a step may name, comes once at the top of the reply, inside `act` in a `drive`.

perform_export.what: Write the session's calls since `start` as a script that replays them and checks their answers, with no model.
perform_export.ask: Save what we did in this session as a script that replays and checks it without you.
perform_export.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, in a session that ran to the first brick hit, forced a register and stepped.
perform_export.reads: Fifteen calls replay, four of them as checks, and 13 calls were left out. `cut` is unavailable because nothing ended the script early; `kept` says the script is now a candidate for `promote`.

arguments.dest: The `.json` file to write: absolute, or starting with `~`. Refused when it exists, unless `overwrite`.
arguments.overwrite: `true` replaces a `dest` that is already there. Left out, an existing file is refused.

returns.steps: How many calls the script replays; `path` is the file written.
returns.checks: How many of them compare a reading with its `recorded` values, the answer the session got.
returns.dropped: The last 40 calls left out (reads the script does not check, refused calls, calls that change nothing), each with its `call`, `op` and `why`; `dropped_total` counts all.
returns.cut: The call the script ends before, with its `call`, `op` and `why`. It is `available: false` when every call a replay can run was kept.
returns.replay: The command that [replays the script](../../REFERENCE.md#from-a-session-to-a-test-that-replays-itself), run from this server's repository. It exits 0 when every step gave its `recorded` values again.
returns.kept: Says the script was saved as a candidate for `promote`: it reads "N saved for `promote`", and names a repository that has no `.scry/` folder yet.

refuses: A `dest` that does not end in `.json`, is a directory, or exists without `overwrite` (`bad_argument`).
No `start` that succeeded, one that was cancelled, or no call left that a replay could run (`no_recording`).
why: The script keeps the calls that move the program and a few readings as checks, each with the answer it got as `recorded`. A call that left the program at a new stop is checked on that stop's `regs` and `frame`.

The script ends at the first call no replay can reach. A `resume`, or a run that the clock or a `stop` ended, stops the cpu at a point inside its frame that no replayed run reaches. Every later stop would inherit the shift.

So move with `run_for`, `run_to` and `step`, which stop at the same point on every run, and keep `resume` for the end. Leave the `dest` of a step that writes a file empty: a file the session named is still there on replay, and the step is refused.
why_more: When the frames are known, `cut` says how many the run took, and a `run_for` of that many replays it up to that frame's start. The script also ends at a call with no reply, a refusal after the program moved, and a program found elsewhere than the call before left it.

A `screen_wait` that found its text becomes a `run_for` of as many frames as it polled, which a replay reaches. A `send_keys` or `send_mouse` to a stopped program is kept as a step: it runs frame by frame to a stop a replay reaches.

- A `debug` command the script keeps is never checked against its answer, and a `state_write(method="load")` is checked against nothing either.
- The file names what a replay needs: `needs.states`, the saved states it loads and does not save itself.
- And `needs.declarations`: the breakpoints and watches saved when the recorded `start` began, so a replay under others says so before it plays.

drive.what: Send an input as a list of steps, then check the program reacted by waiting for a new line in the log.
drive.ask: Press M and check the game handed the paddle to the mouse: wait for its MOUSE ON line.
drive.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, while it runs, in a session started with a `logfile`.
drive.reads: The summary says a new log line matched `expect` after the key went in. The line itself is under `verify` in the whole reply, with the lines `looked` kept.

arguments.act: The steps to run, in the shape `perform` takes: `{"op": <tool>, ...}`. Required, and never empty.
arguments.expect: A regular expression: the log line that shows the program reacted, waited for after the steps. Left out, nothing is checked and `verify` says `checked: false`.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the `expect` line. Left out, 5 seconds; given without `expect`, the call is refused.
arguments.pattern: A regular expression that picks which new log lines `looked` shows. It changes nothing in the check; left out, every line.
arguments.limit: How many of those lines `looked` shows, the newest: 1 to 400. Left out, 40.
arguments.settle_seconds: As in `perform`. With `expect`, the last step's stop is not waited for: waiting for the line is the wait.
arguments.summaries: As in `perform`: `true` cuts each step's reply but the last to a short row.

returns.act: What the steps did, in the fields of a `perform` reply: `ran`, `steps_completed`, `failed_at` and the rest.
returns.verify: The check: `checked` says whether one ran and `seen` whether the line came, with the `line`, the `verdict` (`TARGET` or `TIMEOUT`) and `waited_s`.
returns.looked: Under `guest`, the newest `lines` the program wrote since the steps began that match `pattern`, with `lines_total` and `truncated`.

refuses: `seconds` without `expect`, or an empty `act` (`bad_argument`).
A bad step or argument in `act`, before anything runs; `operations` lists the tools a step may name (`bad_argument`).
A session started without a `logfile`, which leaves no log to read (`no_channel`).
A step that answers INVALID (`step_failed`).
The program stopped at the debugger without the line: a stopped program writes nothing more. The reply adds `last_stop` (`wait_stopped`).
A refusal of the steps themselves comes back with its own code, such as `not_stopped`, `session_broken` or `diverged`.
why: The log is marked once, before the first step, so a line written before the input is never taken for a reaction.

The log is the program's own: the lines it writes to port E9, kept in the session's `logfile`. Steps that end with the program stopped get one read of it, not a wait; `send_keys` and `send_mouse` with `expect` do wait, frame by frame.

`checked` says a check ran and `seen` that the line came; neither is `verified`, which elsewhere means a value read back equal to the one sent. A still of the screen needs a recording and `ffmpeg`, so `capture_frame` takes it.
why_more: `verify` also carries `expected`, `seen_before_waiting`, `lines_before` and `lines_total`; on a `TIMEOUT`, `arrived_during`, `lines_examined` and a `note`; after a stop, `stopped_during_wait` and `lines_on_disk`. `why` explains `checked: false`; `available: false` means the steps ran out their own wait. `looked.guest` adds `lines_written`, `since_mark` and `pattern`.

promote.what: Review what the session learned and write the entries you approve into the repository's `.scry/` folder.
promote.ask: Show me what this session would save into the repository's `.scry/`, without writing anything.
promote.on: On [Bricks](../../demos/bricks/README.md), the game this repository builds, in a session started with the game's `conf` and `cwd`. The repository already has a `.scry/` folder.
promote.reads: The review read the repository's own `.scry/` folder and wrote nothing. `total_bytes` is the size of the candidates that would change it, and `store_bytes` the folder's size with them written.

arguments.dry_run: `true` reviews: it lists every candidate and writes nothing. It cannot be given together with `entries`.
arguments.entries: The entries to write, each `<kind>/<name>` with a kind of `start`, `maps` or `perform`. Only these are written.
arguments.names: A new name for an entry as it is written, as `{"<kind>/<name>": "<new name>"}`. Left out, each keeps its name.
arguments.root: The repository whose `.scry/` folder takes every entry of the call: absolute, or starting with `~`. Left out, each entry goes to its own repository.

returns.candidates: A review's list. Each `entry` has its `kind`, `name`, `file`, `bytes` and `change` (`new` or `update`), an update its `diff`, and one from another repository says `from`.
returns.unchanged: A review's entries that already equal their file in `.scry/`, so there is nothing to approve.
returns.unwritable: Entries this call cannot write, each with its `reason`: most often a repository with no `.scry/` folder, which a call with `root` creates.
returns.written: An approval's entries as written, in the fields `candidates` uses.
returns.draft: After an approval, the session's candidates not yet written to `.scry/`.
returns.would_create: What an approval would create that is not there yet: `.scry/`, its `about.json` and its `README.md`. An approval names what it created in `created`.

refuses: Nothing saved yet: no `start`, screen map or exported script of this session is a complete candidate (`needs_call`).
Both `dry_run` and `entries`, or neither (`bad_argument`).
An entry the session did not save, one named twice, or a name in `names` for an entry not in `entries` (`bad_argument`).
Without `root`: no entry with a `.scry/` folder to go to, or entries of two repositories in one call (`bad_argument`).
A name two repositories saved, unless `root` is one of them (`bad_argument`).
Two entries that `names` would write to one file (`bad_argument`).
An entry a review lists as `unwritable` (`bad_argument`).
More entries of one kind, or more bytes, than a `.scry/` folder may hold (`bad_argument`).
A `root` that is relative, is no directory, or names the `.scry/` folder itself (`bad_argument`).
A file the host would not write; the message names what was written before it (`host_failed`).
why: Nothing is written into a repository until a call names the entries to write. The `.scry/` folder is tracked, so every entry is reviewed before it is written, and only an approved call creates the folder. [The `.scry/` folder](../../REFERENCE.md#the-scry-folder) says what it holds.

`dry_run=true` lists each candidate that would change the folder: its file, its size and whether it is new or an update, an update with what changes. It names the candidates that would change nothing, and what an approval would create beside the entries.

An entry belongs to one repository, fixed when it is saved: the one a call read it from, else the current `start`'s. That is its profile's repository, else the one its program runs in: its `cwd` or its `conf`'s directory, up to the nearest directory holding `.scry/`, else `.git`.
why_more: A candidate is saved only when complete: a start profile with the arguments it cannot start without, a screen map its reader parses, a script with a check. A reply that saves one also names each repository with no `.scry/` folder and the `root` to give.

An entry a call loaded (`start(profile=)`, `screen_map_write(method="load")`, `perform(path=)`) gives its name to what is learned next, so saving it again is an update. An update keeps the keys that belong to a run as the file has them.

Every path in an entry is written as a placeholder ([the rule](https://github.com/scry-mcp/scry-core/blob/main/docs/store-paths.md)), so the tracked file reads the same on any machine. `close` names in `draft` what was left unwritten, and the candidates stay until the server ends.

`store` is the `.scry/` folder the call reads or writes, `store_bytes` its size with the entries written, and `total_bytes` the size of the candidates listed. A `diff` holds `added`, `removed` and `changed`, each change with its `path`, `was` and `now`; `changed_total` counts them when the list is cut.

knowledge_find.what: Ask what a number is called on this machine and what its documentation says of it: a DOS or BIOS call, a DOS error.
knowledge_find.on: Any session, or none: the base answers from the server's own files.
knowledge_find.ask: What does INT 21h with AH=4Ch do?
knowledge_find.reads: One entry matches, so `entries` gives it whole: what Ralf Brown's list says first, each row with DOSBox-X's verdict, then DOSBox-X's notes. `id=ibm-pc:call:0x21/0x4C#3` answers one row, with links.

arguments.id: An entry's id, such as `ibm-pc:call:0x21/0x4C`, answers it whole. `<id>#<n>` answers its row `n`, with the link that opens each line it cites.
arguments.kind: What the number is: `vector`, `call`, `error`, `port`, `irq`, `memory`, `input`, `device`, `register` or `command`. Left empty, every kind.
arguments.key: The number as a reply prints it: a call is `INT/AH` or `INT/AH/AL`, such as `0x21/0x4C`.
arguments.text: Words looked for in names, aliases and the rows' text. A word ending in `*` matches by prefix.
arguments.device: A device's key: everything that belongs to it.
arguments.scope: `ibm-pc`, the only system this server names. Left empty, all.
arguments.limit: How many entries are listed: 1 to 50. Left out, 10.

returns.entries: One match, or an `id`, gives the entry whole: its `rows`, then `sources`, each place once with its link. More matches list each entry's `id` and `name`.
returns.examined: How many entries were searched, so a zero says what it is a zero of.
returns.unconfirmed: Present when entries match that the base holds and does not answer yet: their ids.
returns.nearest: When nothing matched: the entries next to the number or the words.

refuses: None of `id`, `kind`, `key`, `text`, `device` (`bad_argument`).
A `key` that is no number of that `kind`, or a `scope` the server does not hold (`bad_argument`).
An `id` or a `device` the base does not hold (`unknown_ref`).
why: A row says what the documentation states, with `verdicts` saying whether DOSBox-X does it; a note (`vs`) says what DOSBox-X does otherwise. Each row's `cites` says where its lines are and never copies them. Past 24 rows the reply is cut, notes first, and says `rows_total`; an entry no official document covers says so in `source`. The base is the server's own copy: it answers while the program runs.
